translation.name: World English Bible
translation.notice: Scripture quotations are from the World English Bible Classic, in the public domain. Original summaries and reflections are separately labeled.

lessons.title: Build on the rock
lessons.subtitle: Hearing becomes living.
lessons.artworkAlt: A stone house on a large rock foundation beside a stream, under clearing storm clouds.
lessons.summary: Jesus describes two builders. One builds on rock; the other builds on sand. Rain, floods, and wind strike both houses. Only the house on rock stands. Jesus connects the foundations to how people respond to his words.

challenge.prompt: What makes someone like the wise builder?

choices.text: Hearing Jesus’ words and doing them

challenge.explanation: Both builders hear. The difference is putting Jesus’ words into practice.

lessons.takeaway: A strong foundation grows through practiced teaching.
lessons.application: Which teaching of Jesus could you put into practice in one small way today?

verses.text: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house on the rock.
The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.
Everyone who hears these words of mine and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand.
The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house; and it fell—and its fall was great.”

lessons.title: Who is my neighbor?
lessons.subtitle: Compassion takes the next step.
lessons.artworkAlt: A traveler bandages an injured man’s arm beside a road, with a loaded donkey nearby.
lessons.summary: Asked who counts as a neighbor, Jesus tells of a wounded traveler. A priest and a Levite pass by. A Samaritan stops, tends the wounds, brings the traveler to an inn, and pays for further care.

challenge.prompt: Put the Samaritan’s care in order.
challenge.explanation: His compassion becomes practical care. Jesus ends by inviting his listener to do likewise.

lessons.takeaway: Being a neighbor means showing mercy.
lessons.application: Who near you could use a practical act of care today?

verses.text: Behold, a certain lawyer stood up and tested him, saying, “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?”
He said to him, “What is written in the law? How do you read it?”
He answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself.”
He said to him, “You have answered correctly. Do this, and you will live.”
But he, desiring to justify himself, asked Jesus, “Who is my neighbor?”
Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion,
came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
On the next day, when he departed, he took out two denarii, gave them to the host, and said to him, ‘Take care of him. Whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay you when I return.’
Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?”
He said, “He who showed mercy on him.” Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”

lessons.title: Look at yourself first
lessons.subtitle: Begin with honest attention.
lessons.artworkAlt: A large timber beam and a tiny curled wood shaving in a sunlit ancient carpentry workshop.
lessons.summary: Jesus warns against judging others while overlooking our own faults. He pictures a person noticing a speck in someone else’s eye while carrying a beam in their own. First dealing with the beam allows them to see clearly enough to help.

challenge.prompt: What does Jesus say to address first?

choices.text: The beam in your own eye

challenge.explanation: Jesus places honest self-examination before correcting someone else.

lessons.takeaway: Humility changes how we offer help.
lessons.application: Before your next criticism, what might you need to examine in yourself?

verses.text: “Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged.
For with whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged; and with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you.
Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?
Or how will you tell your brother, ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye,’ and behold, the beam is in your own eye?
You hypocrite! First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.

lessons.title: Receiving and giving mercy
lessons.subtitle: Remember what you have received.
lessons.artworkAlt: A seated older man extends an open hand toward a grateful servant beside an unrolled scroll.
lessons.summary: Peter asks how often to forgive. Jesus tells of a servant whose enormous debt is forgiven. That servant then imprisons another over a much smaller debt. The king calls him back and condemns his refusal to show the mercy he received.

challenge.prompt: Put the parable’s events in order.

choices.text: The king calls him to account
The king forgives the huge debt

challenge.explanation: After receiving mercy, the servant refuses to extend it. The king confronts that contradiction.

lessons.takeaway: Received mercy calls for a merciful response.
lessons.application: Recall a time someone showed you patience. How might that shape an ordinary interaction today?

verses.text: Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?”
Jesus said to him, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.
Therefore the Kingdom of Heaven is like a certain king who wanted to settle accounts with his servants.
When he had begun to settle, one was brought to him who owed him ten thousand talents.
But because he couldn’t pay, his lord commanded him to be sold, with his wife, his children, and all that he had, and payment to be made.
The servant therefore fell down and knelt before him, saying, ‘Lord, have patience with me, and I will repay you all!’
The lord of that servant, being moved with compassion, released him and forgave him the debt.
“But that servant went out and found one of his fellow servants who owed him one hundred denarii, and he grabbed him and took him by the throat, saying, ‘Pay me what you owe!’
“So his fellow servant fell down at his feet and begged him, saying, ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you!’
He would not, but went and cast him into prison until he should pay back that which was due.
So when his fellow servants saw what was done, they were exceedingly sorry, and came and told their lord all that was done.
Then his lord called him in and said to him, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me.
Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?’
His lord was angry, and delivered him to the tormentors until he should pay all that was due to him.
So my heavenly Father will also do to you, if you don’t each forgive your brother from your hearts for his misdeeds.”

lessons.title: What am I storing up?
lessons.subtitle: Life is more than what we possess.
lessons.artworkAlt: A sunlit stone granary filled with clay jars, sacks, and overflowing baskets of grain.
lessons.summary: After warning against greed, Jesus tells of a rich man with an abundant harvest. He plans bigger barns and years of ease. But God tells him his life will end that night. Jesus contrasts storing treasure for ourselves with being rich toward God.

challenge.prompt: What does Jesus warn us not to measure life by?
challenge.explanation: More stored goods cannot secure the man’s life. Jesus challenges his misplaced confidence.

lessons.takeaway: Possessions are a poor measure of life.
lessons.application: What could being rich toward God look like in one small choice today?

verses.text: One of the multitude said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”
But he said to him, “Man, who made me a judge or an arbitrator over you?”
He said to them, “Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.”
He spoke a parable to them, saying, “The ground of a certain rich man produced abundantly.
He reasoned within himself, saying, ‘What will I do, because I don’t have room to store my crops?’
He said, ‘This is what I will do. I will pull down my barns, build bigger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods.
I will tell my soul, “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years. Take your ease, eat, drink, and be merry.” ’
“But God said to him, ‘You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared—whose will they be?’
So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.”

lessons.title: Make room for the word
lessons.subtitle: Growth takes patient attention.
lessons.artworkAlt: A farmer scatters seed beside a path, stones, thorny ground, and a green field.
lessons.summary: A farmer scatters seed on a road, rocky ground, thorny ground, and good soil. Jesus explains that the farmer sows the word. Different ground pictures different responses. The good soil represents people who hear the word, accept it, and bear fruit.

challenge.prompt: What marks the good soil in Jesus’ explanation?

choices.text: Feeling joy only at the start

challenge.explanation: Hearing becomes a fruitful response when people accept the word. Other concerns can crowd it out.

lessons.takeaway: Make room for the word to take root.
lessons.application: What small distraction could you set aside to give this passage your attention again?

verses.text: Again he began to teach by the seaside. A great multitude was gathered to him, so that he entered into a boat in the sea and sat down. All the multitude were on the land by the sea.
He taught them many things in parables, and told them in his teaching,
“Listen! Behold, the farmer went out to sow.
As he sowed, some seed fell by the road, and the birds came and devoured it.
Others fell on the rocky ground, where it had little soil, and immediately it sprang up, because it had no depth of soil.
When the sun had risen, it was scorched; and because it had no root, it withered away.
Others fell among the thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded no fruit.
Others fell into the good ground and yielded fruit, growing up and increasing. Some produced thirty times, some sixty times, and some one hundred times as much.”
He said, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”
When he was alone, those who were around him with the twelve asked him about the parables.
He said to them, “To you is given the mystery of God’s Kingdom, but to those who are outside, all things are done in parables,
that ‘seeing they may see and not perceive, and hearing they may hear and not understand, lest perhaps they should turn again, and their sins should be forgiven them.’ ”
He said to them, “Don’t you understand this parable? How will you understand all of the parables?
The farmer sows the word.
The ones by the road are the ones where the word is sown; and when they have heard, immediately Satan comes and takes away the word which has been sown in them.
These in the same way are those who are sown on the rocky places, who, when they have heard the word, immediately receive it with joy.
They have no root in themselves, but are short-lived. When oppression or persecution arises because of the word, immediately they stumble.
Others are those who are sown among the thorns. These are those who have heard the word,
and the cares of this age, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things entering in choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful.
Those which were sown on the good ground are those who hear the word, accept it, and bear fruit, some thirty times, some sixty times, and some one hundred times.”

lessons.title: The lost sheep
lessons.subtitle: There is joy in being found.
lessons.artworkAlt: A smiling shepherd carries a sheep across his shoulders at sunset, with a flock on the hillside.
lessons.summary: Some listeners complain that Jesus welcomes sinners. He answers with a shepherd’s story: one sheep is lost, so the shepherd searches until he finds it. He carries it home with joy and invites others to celebrate.

challenge.prompt: Put the shepherd’s actions in order.
challenge.explanation: Jesus connects the shepherd’s joy with heaven’s joy over one sinner who repents.

lessons.takeaway: Turning back is met with joy.
lessons.application: What is one small way you would like to turn toward God today?

verses.text: Now all the tax collectors and sinners were coming close to him to hear him.
The Pharisees and the scribes murmured, saying, “This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them.”
He told them this parable:
“Which of you men, if you had one hundred sheep and lost one of them, wouldn’t leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost, until he found it?
When he has found it, he carries it on his shoulders, rejoicing.
When he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost!’
I tell you that even so there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance.

lessons.title: Joseph’s dream
lessons.subtitle: Courage for the next faithful step.
lessons.artworkAlt: Joseph sleeps on a woven mat beside a woodworking bench, with warm doorway light and a moonlit village outside.
lessons.summary: Joseph plans to end his engagement quietly when Mary is found pregnant. An angel tells him the child is from the Holy Spirit and will save his people. Joseph takes Mary as his wife and names the child Jesus.

challenge.prompt: Put Joseph’s response in order.
challenge.explanation: Joseph acts on the angel’s message, receiving Mary and giving the child the name connected with his saving mission.

lessons.takeaway: Faithful obedience can begin with one courageous next step.
lessons.application: Is there a clear responsibility you could approach with greater kindness and courage today?

verses.text: Now the birth of Jesus Christ was like this: After his mother, Mary, was engaged to Joseph, before they came together, she was found pregnant by the Holy Spirit.
Joseph, her husband, being a righteous man, and not willing to make her a public example, intended to put her away secretly.

But when he thought about these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, “Joseph, son of David, don’t be afraid to take to yourself Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit.
She shall give birth to a son. You shall name him Jesus, for it is he who shall save his people from their sins.”
Now all this has happened that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet, saying,
“Behold, the virgin shall be with child, and shall give birth to a son. They shall call his name Immanuel,” which is, being interpreted, “God with us.”
Joseph arose from his sleep, and did as the angel of the Lord commanded him, and took his wife to himself;
and didn’t know her sexually until she had given birth to her firstborn son. He named him Jesus.

lessons.title: Visitors follow the star
lessons.subtitle: A journey becomes worship.
lessons.artworkAlt: Travelers carrying small gift containers approach a lamplit Judean house beneath a bright star.
lessons.summary: Wise visitors travel from the east seeking the newborn king. A star leads them to the child’s house. They rejoice, worship, and offer gifts. Warned in a dream, they return home by another route instead of reporting to Herod.

challenge.prompt: Put the visitors’ journey in order.
challenge.explanation: The visitors honor Jesus, then heed the warning about Herod. Their return route changes after their worship.

lessons.takeaway: Seeking Jesus leads these travelers to worship and obedience.
lessons.application: What might help you make room for a moment of attentive worship today?

verses.text: Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod, behold, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem, saying,
“Where is he who is born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the east, and have come to worship him.”
When King Herod heard it, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.
Gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he asked them where the Christ would be born.
They said to him, “In Bethlehem of Judea, for this is written through the prophet,
‘You Bethlehem, land of Judah, are in no way least among the princes of Judah; for out of you shall come a governor who shall shepherd my people, Israel.’ ”
Then Herod secretly called the wise men, and learned from them exactly what time the star appeared.
He sent them to Bethlehem, and said, “Go and search diligently for the young child. When you have found him, bring me word, so that I also may come and worship him.”
They, having heard the king, went their way; and behold, the star, which they saw in the east, went before them until it came and stood over where the young child was.
When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.
They came into the house and saw the young child with Mary, his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Opening their treasures, they offered to him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.
Being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their own country another way.

lessons.title: A refuge in Egypt
lessons.subtitle: A family takes the road to safety.
lessons.artworkAlt: Joseph leads a donkey carrying a cloaked Mary along a moonlit road toward palms and distant Egyptian buildings.
lessons.summary: Warned in a dream, Joseph takes Jesus and Mary to Egypt. Herod kills young children in Bethlehem. After Herod dies, another dream leads the family back; Joseph settles in Nazareth after a further warning.

challenge.prompt: Put the family’s journey in order.
challenge.explanation: Joseph responds to danger with protective action. Matthew also acknowledges the terrible grief of families harmed by Herod.

lessons.takeaway: This journey holds both protective care and profound grief.
lessons.application: Could you offer practical kindness to someone facing displacement or a difficult move?

verses.text: Now when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying, “Arise and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and stay there until I tell you, for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him.”
He arose and took the young child and his mother by night and departed into Egypt,
and was there until the death of Herod, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet, saying, “Out of Egypt I called my son.”

Then Herod, when he saw that he was mocked by the wise men, was exceedingly angry, and sent out and killed all the male children who were in Bethlehem and in all the surrounding countryside, from two years old and under, according to the exact time which he had learned from the wise men.
Then that which was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled, saying,
“A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, weeping and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children; she wouldn’t be comforted, because they are no more.”
But when Herod was dead, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying,
“Arise and take the young child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel, for those who sought the young child’s life are dead.”
He arose and took the young child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel.
But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in the place of his father, Herod, he was afraid to go there. Being warned in a dream, he withdrew into the region of Galilee,
and came and lived in a city called Nazareth; that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophets that he will be called a Nazarene.

lessons.title: Prepare the way
lessons.subtitle: A changed direction bears fruit.
lessons.artworkAlt: John the Baptist, in rough clothing with a leather belt, speaks to attentive adults beside the Jordan River.
lessons.summary: John preaches in the wilderness, calling people to repent because God’s kingdom is near. Crowds come to the Jordan. John warns that ancestry is no substitute for a changed life and points toward someone mightier than himself.

challenge.prompt: What does John ask repentance to produce?
challenge.explanation: John calls for a response visible in how people live, rather than confidence in their ancestry or religious status.

lessons.takeaway: Turning toward God should shape how we live today.
lessons.application: What small change in direction could become visible in one action today?

verses.text: In those days, John the Baptizer came, preaching in the wilderness of Judea, saying,
“Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand!”
For this is he who was spoken of by Isaiah the prophet, saying, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness, make the way of the Lord ready! Make his paths straight!”
Now John himself wore clothing made of camel’s hair with a leather belt around his waist. His food was locusts and wild honey.
Then people from Jerusalem, all of Judea, and all the region around the Jordan went out to him.
They were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins.
But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming for his baptism, he said to them, “You offspring of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance!
Don’t think to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham for our father,’ for I tell you that God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones.
Even now the ax lies at the root of the trees. Therefore every tree that doesn’t produce good fruit is cut down, and cast into the fire.
“I indeed baptize you in water for repentance, but he who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit.
His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor. He will gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn up with unquenchable fire.”

lessons.title: Jesus is baptized
lessons.subtitle: Listen to the Father’s welcome.
lessons.artworkAlt: A white dove descends above a quiet bend of the Jordan River, with rippling water and reeds in warm morning light.
lessons.summary: Jesus comes to John at the Jordan for baptism. John hesitates, but Jesus tells him to allow it. As Jesus comes from the water, the Spirit descends like a dove and a heavenly voice identifies him as the beloved Son.

challenge.prompt: What does the heavenly voice say about Jesus?

choices.text: He is a prophet like Elijah

challenge.explanation: The voice identifies Jesus as the beloved Son and expresses delight in him as his public ministry begins.

lessons.takeaway: The scene directs our attention to Jesus’ beloved identity.
lessons.application: As you read the passage, which detail helps you attend to who Jesus is?

verses.text: Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him.
But John would have hindered him, saying, “I need to be baptized by you, and you come to me?”
But Jesus, answering, said to him, “Allow it now, for this is the fitting way for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he allowed him.
Jesus, when he was baptized, went up directly from the water: and behold, the heavens were opened to him. He saw the Spirit of God descending as a dove, and coming on him.
Behold, a voice out of the heavens said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.”

lessons.title: Tested in the wilderness
lessons.subtitle: Keep God at the center.
lessons.artworkAlt: Rounded stones sit along a barren wilderness path beneath a high rocky ridge and a pale dawn sky.
lessons.summary: After fasting in the wilderness, Jesus faces three temptations: turn stones into bread, leap from the temple, and gain kingdoms through false worship. He answers each with Scripture, refusing to test God or worship anyone else.

challenge.prompt: Put Matthew’s three temptations in order.
challenge.explanation: Jesus responds with Scripture, refusing shortcuts that would turn him from trusting and serving God alone in the wilderness.

lessons.takeaway: Faithfulness holds to God when tempting shortcuts promise more.
lessons.application: Is there a tempting shortcut you could pause and examine in light of Jesus’ teaching?

verses.text: Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.
When he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was hungry afterward.
The tempter came and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.”
But he answered, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.’ ”
Then the devil took him into the holy city. He set him on the pinnacle of the temple,

and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you,’ and, ‘On their hands they will bear you up, so that you don’t dash your foot against a stone.’ ”
Jesus said to him, “Again, it is written, ‘You shall not test the Lord, your God.’ ”
Again, the devil took him to an exceedingly high mountain, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory.
He said to him, “I will give you all of these things, if you will fall down and worship me.”
Then Jesus said to him, “Get behind me, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only.’ ”
Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and served him.

lessons.title: Called from the nets
lessons.subtitle: An invitation on an ordinary shore.
lessons.artworkAlt: Two fishermen walk inland from fishing nets and wooden boats on the shore of Galilee.
lessons.summary: Walking beside Galilee, Jesus calls Peter and Andrew while they fish. They leave their nets and follow. Farther along, he calls James and John as they mend nets with their father; they also leave the boat and follow him.

challenge.prompt: How do both pairs of brothers respond?
challenge.explanation: Both pairs respond promptly to Jesus’ call. Their ordinary work becomes the setting for a new direction of discipleship.

lessons.takeaway: Jesus’ invitation reaches people in the middle of work.
lessons.application: Where in an ordinary task could you pay closer attention to following Jesus today?

verses.text: Walking by the sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers: Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew, his brother, casting a net into the sea; for they were fishermen.
He said to them, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers for men.”
They immediately left their nets and followed him.
Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets. He called them.
They immediately left the boat and their father, and followed him.

lessons.title: The Beatitudes
lessons.subtitle: Blessing seen through Jesus’ teaching.
lessons.artworkAlt: A group of adults listens thoughtfully on a green hillside overlooking Galilee.
lessons.summary: Jesus teaches on a mountainside, naming the merciful, mourners, and the gentle as blessed. He says peacemakers will be called children of God. He also speaks hope to those persecuted for righteousness, beyond public success or comfort.

challenge.prompt: Who will be called children of God?
challenge.explanation: Jesus names peacemakers as children of God. His blessings challenge assumptions that happiness depends on status or comfort.

lessons.takeaway: Jesus honors mercy and peace beyond the world’s applause.
lessons.application: What small act of peacemaking is within your reach today?

verses.text: Seeing the multitudes, he went up onto the mountain. When he had sat down, his disciples came to him.
He opened his mouth and taught them, saying,
“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.
Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.
Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth.
Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.
Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.
Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.
Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.
Blessed are those who have been persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven.
“Blessed are you when people reproach you, persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
Rejoice, and be exceedingly glad, for great is your reward in heaven. For that is how they persecuted the prophets who were before you.

lessons.title: Salt and light
lessons.subtitle: Goodness points beyond ourselves.
lessons.artworkAlt: A clay oil lamp glows beside a bowl of salt, with a lit hilltop town beyond the stone ledge.
lessons.summary: Jesus calls his disciples salt and light. He pictures a city on a hill and a lamp placed where it lights a home. Their good works should be visible so that people give glory to their Father in heaven.

challenge.prompt: What should seeing these good works lead to?
challenge.explanation: The light serves others and points toward the Father. Visibility matters here because of whom the good works honor.

lessons.takeaway: Let useful kindness point beyond yourself toward the Father.
lessons.application: Could one ordinary act of helpfulness make someone’s day brighter?

verses.text: “You are the salt of the earth, but if the salt has lost its flavor, with what will it be salted? It is then good for nothing, but to be cast out and trodden under the feet of men.
“You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.
Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house.
Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

lessons.title: Make peace first
lessons.subtitle: Repair deserves your attention.
lessons.artworkAlt: Two adult neighbors clasp forearms and speak face to face in a sunlit courtyard.
lessons.summary: Jesus warns that anger and contempt matter, not only outward violence. He imagines someone remembering a damaged relationship while offering a gift. That person should leave the gift, seek reconciliation, and then return to offer it.

challenge.prompt: Put Jesus’ instructions about the gift in order.

choices.text: Leave the gift at the altar

challenge.explanation: Jesus gives repairing a relationship priority over continuing the offering. Worship does not excuse leaving our own harm unaddressed.

lessons.takeaway: Take responsibility for harm before carrying on as usual.
lessons.application: Is there a small wrong of yours you could acknowledge, when contact is safe and appropriate?

verses.text: “You have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not murder;’ and ‘Whoever murders will be in danger of the judgment.’

But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother without a cause will be in danger of the judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca!’ will be in danger of the council. Whoever says, ‘You fool!’ will be in danger of the fire of Gehenna.
“If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you,
leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
Agree with your adversary quickly while you are with him on the way; lest perhaps the prosecutor deliver you to the judge, and the judge deliver you to the officer, and you be cast into prison.
Most certainly I tell you, you shall by no means get out of there until you have paid the last penny.

lessons.title: Let your yes be yes
lessons.subtitle: Simple words can carry integrity.
lessons.artworkAlt: Two neighbors speak face to face beneath an olive tree in a sunlit courtyard.
lessons.summary: Jesus teaches about oaths, warning against swearing by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, or one’s own head. These things are not ours to control. He directs his listeners toward plain, reliable speech: let a yes be yes and a no be no.

challenge.prompt: What kind of speech does Jesus call for?

choices.text: A plain, dependable yes or no
Unclear promises that keep options open

challenge.explanation: Jesus calls for straightforward truthfulness rather than elaborate guarantees. Honest speech should not need impressive objects to make it credible.

lessons.takeaway: Let dependable words carry the weight of your promises.
lessons.application: Is there a promise you should keep, clarify, or honestly correct today?

verses.text: “Again you have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not make false vows, but shall perform to the Lord your vows,’
but I tell you, don’t swear at all: neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God;
nor by the earth, for it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King.
Neither shall you swear by your head, for you can’t make one hair white or black.
But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.

lessons.title: Love your enemies
lessons.subtitle: Prayer can reach beyond your circle.
lessons.artworkAlt: A woman offers a water cup to a seated traveler beneath an olive tree as sunlight breaks through distant rain.
lessons.summary: Jesus tells his listeners to love enemies and pray for those who mistreat them. He points to the Father, who gives sunshine and rain to both good and evil people. Loving only those who love us is too narrow.

challenge.prompt: Whom does Jesus explicitly tell us to pray for?

choices.text: Only friends who return our kindness
Those who mistreat or persecute us
People who already agree with us

challenge.explanation: The Father’s generosity reaches beyond those who deserve it. Jesus calls his followers toward love wider than mutual affection.

lessons.takeaway: Love can seek another’s good while keeping wise boundaries.
lessons.application: Could you pray for someone difficult from a safe distance, without excusing harm?

verses.text: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’
But I tell you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you,
that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust.
For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Don’t even the tax collectors do the same?
If you only greet your friends, what more do you do than others? Don’t even the tax collectors do the same?
Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.

lessons.title: Giving without applause
lessons.subtitle: Care does not need an audience.
lessons.artworkAlt: A hand leaves a tied pouch beside bread and pottery at a humble doorway.
lessons.summary: Jesus warns against giving to the needy for an audience. Some make their generosity conspicuous to gain praise. Instead, he tells his listeners to give quietly, trusting their Father to see the care that other people may never notice.

challenge.prompt: What motive does Jesus warn against?

choices.text: Giving in order to gain praise

challenge.explanation: The warning concerns giving to be admired. Jesus turns attention from the giver’s reputation toward the Father who sees.

lessons.takeaway: Quiet generosity can care deeply without collecting public credit.
lessons.application: Is there a discreet act of generosity you could offer without seeking recognition?

verses.text: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.

Therefore, when you do merciful deeds, don’t sound a trumpet before yourself, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may get glory from men. Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward.
But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does,
so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.

lessons.title: Learning to pray
lessons.subtitle: Bring your needs to the Father.
lessons.artworkAlt: A loaf of bread rests beside a clay water cup in a quiet room with a closed wooden door.
lessons.summary: Jesus teaches prayer that seeks the Father rather than an audience. His model prayer honors God’s name and kingdom, asks for daily bread and deliverance, and links receiving forgiveness with forgiving others. The Father already knows his children’s needs.

challenge.prompt: What ordinary need appears in Jesus’ model prayer?
challenge.explanation: Jesus includes daily needs alongside God’s kingdom and forgiveness. Prayer can be sincere and direct because the Father knows.

lessons.takeaway: Bring everyday needs to God with honesty and trust.
lessons.application: Which part of this prayer could you pause over in your own words today?

verses.text: “When you pray, you shall not be as the hypocrites, for they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen by men. Most certainly, I tell you, they have received their reward.
But you, when you pray, enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.
In praying, don’t use vain repetitions as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard for their much speaking.
Therefore don’t be like them, for your Father knows what things you need before you ask him.
Pray like this: “ ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.
Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us today our daily bread.
Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.’
“For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.
But if you don’t forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

lessons.title: Fasting in secret
lessons.subtitle: Sincerity matters more than display.
lessons.artworkAlt: A clean linen cloth, small oil vessel, and basin of water sit beside a simple stone washstand.
lessons.summary: Jesus describes people making their fasting obvious through gloomy faces. He tells his listeners to wash and care for their appearance instead. Fasting should be directed toward the Father, who sees in secret, rather than performed for human attention.

challenge.prompt: What does Jesus tell a person fasting to do?

choices.text: Announce how long they have fasted

challenge.explanation: Jesus redirects fasting away from public admiration and toward the Father. The passage emphasizes sincerity rather than visible discomfort.

lessons.takeaway: Let devotion be sincere even when nobody else notices.
lessons.application: What could help one practice of devotion become less about how others see you?

verses.text: “Moreover when you fast, don’t be like the hypocrites, with sad faces. For they disfigure their faces that they may be seen by men to be fasting. Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward.
But you, when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face,
so that you are not seen by men to be fasting, but by your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you.

lessons.title: Treasure in heaven
lessons.subtitle: Notice what holds your heart.
lessons.artworkAlt: An open chest of coins rests in the shade beside a doorway overlooking a sunlit path.
lessons.summary: Jesus contrasts vulnerable earthly treasure with treasure in heaven. What we treasure draws our hearts. He also pictures the eye as a lamp and warns that divided loyalty cannot last: a person cannot serve both God and wealth.

challenge.prompt: Which two masters does Jesus say we cannot serve?
challenge.explanation: Jesus challenges wealth’s claim to our ultimate loyalty. His contrast asks what directs the heart, not merely what we own.

lessons.takeaway: Let what you treasure reflect whom you want to serve.
lessons.application: What small use of time or resources could express your priorities more clearly?

verses.text: “Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal;
but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal;
for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
“The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light.
But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!
“No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.

lessons.title: Birds and flowers
lessons.subtitle: Attend to today with trust.
lessons.artworkAlt: Small birds perch among grasses and pale wildflowers on a sunlit Galilean hillside.
lessons.summary: Jesus points to birds that are fed and flowers clothed with beauty. The Father knows his listeners’ needs. He calls them to seek God’s kingdom and righteousness, and to attend to today instead of carrying tomorrow’s troubles in advance.

challenge.prompt: What does Jesus say to seek first?

choices.text: Enough supplies to prevent every worry

challenge.explanation: Jesus invites trust in the Father’s care and attention to today. He directs priorities toward God’s kingdom and righteousness.

lessons.takeaway: Receive today with trust, one manageable step at a time.
lessons.application: Could you notice one ordinary sign of care and choose one manageable task for today?

verses.text: Therefore I tell you, don’t be anxious for your life: what you will eat, or what you will drink; nor yet for your body, what you will wear. Isn’t life more than food, and the body more than clothing?
See the birds of the sky, that they don’t sow, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns. Your heavenly Father feeds them. Aren’t you of much more value than they?
“Which of you by being anxious, can add one moment to his lifespan?
Why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They don’t toil, neither do they spin,
yet I tell you that even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these.
But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today exists and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, won’t he much more clothe you, you of little faith?
“Therefore don’t be anxious, saying, ‘What will we eat?’, ‘What will we drink?’ or, ‘With what will we be clothed?’
For the Gentiles seek after all these things; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things.
But seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.
Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.

lessons.title: Ask, seek, and knock
lessons.subtitle: Approach the Father with trust.
lessons.artworkAlt: A hand knocks on a partly open wooden door while a welcoming hand reaches from the lamplit room.
lessons.summary: Jesus invites his listeners to ask, seek, and knock. He compares their heavenly Father with parents who give bread rather than stones. The passage then calls listeners to treat others as they themselves would want to be treated.

challenge.prompt: What does the bread-and-stone picture emphasize?

choices.text: A technique for obtaining every wish
The goodness of the Father’s gifts
A bargain that earns God’s attention

challenge.explanation: The comparison points to the Father’s goodness. It encourages trusting prayer rather than a technique for controlling God’s response.

lessons.takeaway: Ask with trust, and extend thoughtful care to others.
lessons.application: What could you honestly bring to God in prayer today?

verses.text: “Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened for you.
For everyone who asks receives. He who seeks finds. To him who knocks it will be opened.
Or who is there among you who, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone?
Or if he asks for a fish, who will give him a serpent?
If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!
Therefore, whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them; for this is the law and the prophets.

lessons.title: The narrow gate
lessons.subtitle: Choose the direction that leads to life.
lessons.artworkAlt: A narrow stone gateway opens onto a peaceful winding path, while a broad road branches away beyond the foreground.
lessons.summary: Jesus pictures two gates and two roads. A wide gate opens onto a broad way leading to destruction. A narrow gate opens onto the way leading to life. He urges his listeners to enter through the narrow gate.

challenge.prompt: Which way does Jesus say leads to life?

choices.text: The road with the largest crowd
The broad road beyond the wide gate
The way beyond the narrow gate

challenge.explanation: Jesus asks listeners to choose the way leading to life. Popularity alone does not show whether a direction is good.

lessons.takeaway: Consider where a choice leads, beyond how popular it is.
lessons.application: Is there a good choice you could make even if it is not the easiest one?

verses.text: “Enter in by the narrow gate; for the gate is wide and the way is broad that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter in by it.
How narrow is the gate and the way is restricted that leads to life! There are few who find it.

lessons.title: Known by their fruit
lessons.subtitle: Look beyond a reassuring appearance.
lessons.artworkAlt: A fruitful fig tree stands beside a bare tree along a stone wall.
lessons.summary: Jesus warns that false prophets can appear harmless. He compares recognizing them to recognizing trees by their fruit: thorns do not produce grapes, and good trees bear good fruit. Appearances alone cannot settle whether a teacher is trustworthy.

challenge.prompt: How does Jesus say to recognize false prophets?
challenge.explanation: The fruit image shifts attention from appearances to what a teacher produces. Jesus calls for discernment rather than automatic trust.

lessons.takeaway: Let a teacher’s conduct matter alongside persuasive words and appearances.
lessons.application: When you encounter spiritual advice, could you pause to consider both its teaching and its results?

verses.text: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves.
By their fruits you will know them. Do you gather grapes from thorns or figs from thistles?
Even so, every good tree produces good fruit, but the corrupt tree produces evil fruit.
A good tree can’t produce evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree produce good fruit.
Every tree that doesn’t grow good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
Therefore by their fruits you will know them.

lessons.title: Rest for the weary
lessons.subtitle: Learn from a gentle teacher.
lessons.artworkAlt: A wooden yoke rests on a stone wall in the shade of an olive tree.
lessons.summary: Jesus thanks the Father for revealing truth to the lowly and speaks of making the Father known. He then invites weary, burdened people to come to him, take his yoke, and learn from his gentle and humble heart.

challenge.prompt: How does Jesus describe his heart?
challenge.explanation: Jesus’ invitation joins rest with learning from him. His gentleness shapes the discipleship he offers to those who are burdened.

lessons.takeaway: Bring your burdens to the teacher who is gentle.
lessons.application: What burden could you name honestly in a moment of prayer today?

verses.text: At that time, Jesus answered, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants.
Yes, Father, for so it was well-pleasing in your sight.
All things have been delivered to me by my Father. No one knows the Son, except the Father; neither does anyone know the Father, except the Son and he to whom the Son desires to reveal him.
“Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

lessons.title: The mustard seed
lessons.subtitle: Do not dismiss a small beginning.
lessons.artworkAlt: A mustard plant’s branching stems shelter small birds, with a tiny seed visible on a hand in the foreground.
lessons.summary: Jesus compares the kingdom of heaven to a mustard seed planted in a field. The seed begins very small, yet its grown branches become a place where birds settle. The picture moves from an easily overlooked beginning to surprising growth.

challenge.prompt: What happens when the mustard plant has grown?

choices.text: A new seed must be planted
The branches are immediately cut down

challenge.explanation: The parable contrasts a small beginning with substantial growth. Jesus uses the mustard plant to describe the kingdom of heaven.

lessons.takeaway: A small beginning need not reveal the whole outcome.
lessons.application: What small, faithful beginning could you value without demanding immediate results?

verses.text: He set another parable before them, saying, “The Kingdom of Heaven is like a grain of mustard seed which a man took, and sowed in his field,
which indeed is smaller than all seeds. But when it is grown, it is greater than the herbs and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in its branches.”

lessons.title: The hidden yeast
lessons.subtitle: Quiet work can spread far.
lessons.artworkAlt: A woman kneads dough in a wooden trough inside a warmly lit stone kitchen.
lessons.summary: Jesus pictures a woman mixing yeast into a large amount of flour until the whole batch is leavened. This ordinary household image describes the kingdom of heaven. Matthew notes that Jesus uses parables to speak of things long hidden.

challenge.prompt: How much of the batch is eventually leavened?
challenge.explanation: The yeast works through the whole batch. Jesus’ image describes the kingdom’s effect using something small and initially hidden.

lessons.takeaway: Do not overlook what is growing beyond immediate notice.
lessons.application: Where might patience help you notice quiet good that is easy to miss?

verses.text: He spoke another parable to them. “The Kingdom of Heaven is like yeast which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, until it was all leavened.”
Jesus spoke all these things in parables to the multitudes; and without a parable, he didn’t speak to them,
that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophet, saying, “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world.”

lessons.title: Treasure in a field
lessons.subtitle: Joy recognizes something worth everything.
lessons.artworkAlt: A farmer kneels beside an opened clay jar of coins partly buried in a sunlit field.
lessons.summary: Jesus compares the kingdom of heaven to treasure hidden in a field. A man discovers it, hides it again, and joyfully sells everything he owns to buy the field. The discovery changes what he considers worth keeping.

challenge.prompt: Put the man’s actions in order.
challenge.explanation: The man’s joyful response highlights the treasure’s value. Jesus uses the discovery to picture the surpassing worth of the kingdom.

lessons.takeaway: Recognizing great value can reshape what we hold most closely.
lessons.application: What worthwhile priority could receive more of your attention today?

verses.text: “Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like treasure hidden in the field, which a man found and hid. In his joy, he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.

lessons.title: The pearl of great price
lessons.subtitle: The search meets a decisive discovery.
lessons.artworkAlt: A merchant holds a luminous pearl in an open palm above indigo cloth and a small purse.
lessons.summary: Jesus tells of a merchant looking for fine pearls. When the merchant finds one pearl of exceptional value, he sells everything he has and buys it. Jesus places this costly, decisive discovery alongside his teaching about the kingdom of heaven.

challenge.prompt: What is the merchant seeking when he finds the exceptional pearl?
challenge.explanation: The merchant is already seeking fine pearls when he recognizes one of surpassing value. His discovery calls for a decisive response.

lessons.takeaway: Let what is truly valuable guide your daily priorities.
lessons.application: Which less important distraction could you set aside for something you deeply value?

verses.text: “Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who is a merchant seeking fine pearls,
who having found one pearl of great price, he went and sold all that he had and bought it.

lessons.title: Wheat and weeds
lessons.subtitle: Patience protects what is growing.
lessons.artworkAlt: Ripe wheat and darker weeds grow together in a field while a worker waits near the far edge.
lessons.summary: Jesus pictures God’s kingdom through a field where an enemy sows weeds among wheat. Servants offer to pull the weeds, but the farmer refuses: uprooting them could harm the wheat. He tells them to wait until harvest.

challenge.prompt: Why does the farmer delay removing the weeds?

choices.text: He thinks the weeds are useful wheat
He wants to avoid uprooting the wheat
He plans never to separate the plants

challenge.explanation: The farmer’s patience protects the wheat until a real harvest and separation. Waiting does not make the weeds harmless.

lessons.takeaway: Patient discernment considers whom a rushed response could harm.
lessons.application: In an ordinary disagreement, could you pause to consider unintended harm before reacting?

verses.text: He set another parable before them, saying, “The Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field,
but while people slept, his enemy came and sowed darnel weeds also among the wheat, and went away.
But when the blade sprang up and produced grain, then the darnel weeds appeared also.
The servants of the householder came and said to him, ‘Sir, didn’t you sow good seed in your field? Where did these darnel weeds come from?’
“He said to them, ‘An enemy has done this.’ “The servants asked him, ‘Do you want us to go and gather them up?’
“But he said, ‘No, lest perhaps while you gather up the darnel weeds, you root up the wheat with them.

Let both grow together until the harvest, and in the harvest time I will tell the reapers, “First, gather up the darnel weeds, and bind them in bundles to burn them; but gather the wheat into my barn.” ’ ”

lessons.title: Becoming like a child
lessons.subtitle: Greatness begins with humility.
lessons.artworkAlt: A young child stands among seated adults in a sunlit courtyard.
lessons.summary: The disciples ask who is greatest in the kingdom of heaven. Jesus places a child among them and calls them to turn and become like children. He names humility as greatness, welcomes the little ones, and warns against causing them harm.

challenge.prompt: What quality does Jesus connect with greatness?
challenge.explanation: Jesus redirects a contest over rank toward humility. Welcoming little ones matters more than securing a place above others.

lessons.takeaway: Choose humility and welcome over the need to outrank others.
lessons.application: Who could you listen to attentively without trying to prove your own importance?

verses.text: In that hour the disciples came to Jesus, saying, “Who then is greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven?”
Jesus called a little child to himself, and set him in the middle of them
and said, “Most certainly I tell you, unless you turn and become as little children, you will in no way enter into the Kingdom of Heaven.
Whoever therefore humbles himself as this little child is the greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven.
Whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me,
but whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a huge millstone were hung around his neck and that he were sunk in the depths of the sea.

lessons.title: Seeking reconciliation
lessons.subtitle: Speak with care when a relationship breaks.
lessons.artworkAlt: Two adults speak quietly across a courtyard table, with an open gateway nearby and no crowd around them.
lessons.summary: Jesus describes responding when a fellow believer sins against you. Begin by speaking privately; if they listen, the relationship is recovered. If not, involve witnesses and then the community. His teaching takes both restoration and accountability seriously.

challenge.prompt: What is the hoped-for result of the first conversation?
challenge.explanation: Jesus names restored relationship as the goal of a listening response. Further steps show that accountability is not simply abandoned.

lessons.takeaway: Seek restoration with honesty, appropriate support, and wise boundaries.
lessons.application: For a small, safe disagreement, could a respectful conversation help? Serious harm may require outside support.

verses.text: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.
But if he doesn’t listen, take one or two more with you, that at the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.
If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the assembly. If he refuses to hear the assembly also, let him be to you as a Gentile or a tax collector.
Most certainly I tell you, whatever things you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven, and whatever things you release on earth will have been released in heaven.
Again, assuredly I tell you, that if two of you will agree on earth concerning anything that they will ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them.”

lessons.title: Workers in the vineyard
lessons.subtitle: Another person’s generosity need not threaten you.
lessons.artworkAlt: Vineyard workers gather at a stone gateway at sunset while an owner places coins into an open hand.
lessons.summary: A vineyard owner hires workers throughout the day. At evening, late arrivals receive a full day’s wage, and early workers receive the agreed amount. The early workers complain, but the owner defends his generosity toward those who came last.

challenge.prompt: Put the owner’s day in order.

choices.text: Pay the workers in the evening
Hire more workers late in the day

challenge.explanation: The owner keeps his agreement while giving generously to others. The parable challenges resentment when someone else receives unexpected goodness.

lessons.takeaway: Practice receiving goodness without resenting generosity shown to others.
lessons.application: Could you celebrate one good thing someone else has received today?

verses.text: “For the Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who was the master of a household, who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard.
When he had agreed with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard.
He went out about the third hour, and saw others standing idle in the marketplace.
He said to them, ‘You also go into the vineyard, and whatever is right I will give you.’ So they went their way.
Again he went out about the sixth and the ninth hour, and did likewise.
About the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing idle. He said to them, ‘Why do you stand here all day idle?’
“They said to him, ‘Because no one has hired us.’ “He said to them, ‘You also go into the vineyard, and you will receive whatever is right.’
“When evening had come, the lord of the vineyard said to his manager, ‘Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning from the last to the first.’
“When those who were hired at about the eleventh hour came, they each received a denarius.
When the first came, they supposed that they would receive more; and they likewise each received a denarius.
When they received it, they murmured against the master of the household,
saying, ‘These last have spent one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat!’
“But he answered one of them, ‘Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Didn’t you agree with me for a denarius?
Take that which is yours, and go your way. It is my desire to give to this last just as much as to you.
Isn’t it lawful for me to do what I want to with what I own? Or is your eye evil, because I am good?’
So the last will be first, and the first last. For many are called, but few are chosen.”

lessons.title: The two sons
lessons.subtitle: A changed response can become action.
lessons.artworkAlt: An older vineyard owner gestures toward a working son while another son remains beside the house.
lessons.summary: A father asks two sons to work in his vineyard. One refuses, then changes his mind and goes. The other agrees but never goes. Jesus uses their responses to challenge listeners who did not believe John’s call to righteousness.

challenge.prompt: Which son does the father’s will?

choices.text: The one who agrees but never goes
The one who changes his mind and goes
Neither, because first words decide everything

challenge.explanation: The first son’s changed action matters more than his initial refusal. Jesus connects this contrast with responding to John.

lessons.takeaway: A sincere change of direction can become a faithful action.
lessons.application: Is there a good responsibility you initially resisted that you could return to today?

verses.text: But what do you think? A man had two sons, and he came to the first, and said, ‘Son, go work today in my vineyard.’
He answered, ‘I will not,’ but afterward he changed his mind, and went.
He came to the second, and said the same thing. He answered, ‘I’m going, sir,’ but he didn’t go.

Which of the two did the will of his father?” They said to him, “The first.” Jesus said to them, “Most certainly I tell you that the tax collectors and the prostitutes are entering into God’s Kingdom before you.

For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you didn’t believe him; but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. When you saw it, you didn’t even repent afterward, that you might believe him.

lessons.title: Lamps ready for the wedding
lessons.subtitle: Readiness matters while we wait.
lessons.artworkAlt: Glowing clay oil lamps and flasks rest on a courtyard wall near an open, lamplit wedding doorway.
lessons.summary: Ten young women await a bridegroom with lamps. Five bring extra oil; five do not. All sleep during his delay. A midnight cry announces him, and those prepared enter the feast. The others find the door shut.

challenge.prompt: Put the wedding story’s events in order.

choices.text: The bridegroom delays and all sleep
A midnight cry announces his coming

challenge.explanation: All ten sleep; their preparation differs. Jesus urges readiness because his listeners do not know the day or hour.

lessons.takeaway: Let patient readiness shape how you live in the present.
lessons.application: What ordinary faithful responsibility could you attend to while the future remains uncertain?

verses.text: “Then the Kingdom of Heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom.
Five of them were foolish, and five were wise.
Those who were foolish, when they took their lamps, took no oil with them,
but the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps.
Now while the bridegroom delayed, they all slumbered and slept.
But at midnight there was a cry, ‘Behold! The bridegroom is coming! Come out to meet him!’
Then all those virgins arose, and trimmed their lamps.
The foolish said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.’
But the wise answered, saying, ‘What if there isn’t enough for us and you? You go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.’
While they went away to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was shut.
Afterward the other virgins also came, saying, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us.’
But he answered, ‘Most certainly I tell you, I don’t know you.’
Watch therefore, for you don’t know the day nor the hour in which the Son of Man is coming.

lessons.title: Mary receives good news
lessons.subtitle: A question, a promise, a willing response.
lessons.artworkAlt: A woman with open hands sits in a lamplit Nazareth home, with dawn light entering the doorway.
lessons.summary: Gabriel visits Mary in Nazareth and announces that she will bear Jesus, whose kingdom will never end. Mary asks how this can happen. The angel speaks of the Holy Spirit, and Mary responds as God’s servant.

challenge.prompt: How does Mary respond after asking her question?

choices.text: She asks to visit Elizabeth first
She offers herself as God’s servant

challenge.explanation: Mary asks an honest question, hears the angel’s explanation, and expresses willingness to receive what God has spoken.

lessons.takeaway: Honest questions can accompany a willing response to God.
lessons.application: What question would you like to bring honestly to God while you read Scripture?

verses.text: Now in the sixth month, the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth,
to a virgin pledged to be married to a man whose name was Joseph, of David’s house. The virgin’s name was Mary.
Having come in, the angel said to her, “Rejoice, you highly favored one! The Lord is with you. Blessed are you among women!”
But when she saw him, she was greatly troubled at the saying, and considered what kind of salutation this might be.
The angel said to her, “Don’t be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God.
Behold, you will conceive in your womb and give birth to a son, and shall name him ‘Jesus.’
He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give him the throne of his father David,
and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever. There will be no end to his Kingdom.”
Mary said to the angel, “How can this be, seeing I am a virgin?”
The angel answered her, “The Holy Spirit will come on you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore also the holy one who is born from you will be called the Son of God.
Behold, Elizabeth your relative also has conceived a son in her old age; and this is the sixth month with her who was called barren.
For nothing spoken by God is impossible.”
Mary said, “Behold, the servant of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.” Then the angel departed from her.

lessons.title: Mary visits Elizabeth
lessons.subtitle: Encouragement at the doorway.
lessons.artworkAlt: Two women greet each other warmly at the doorway of a stone home in the Judean hill country.
lessons.summary: Mary travels to the hill country and greets Elizabeth. Elizabeth’s baby leaps, and Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, blesses Mary and her child. She celebrates Mary’s belief that the Lord’s words will be fulfilled.

challenge.prompt: What does Elizabeth celebrate about Mary?

choices.text: Her belief in the Lord’s words

challenge.explanation: Elizabeth recognizes God’s work and speaks encouragement. Her blessing specifically names Mary’s trust in what the Lord has said.

lessons.takeaway: Speak encouragement that helps another person remember God’s faithfulness.
lessons.application: Who could you encourage today with something hopeful you have read in Scripture?

verses.text: Mary arose in those days and went into the hill country with haste, into a city of Judah,
and entered into the house of Zacharias and greeted Elizabeth.
When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the baby leaped in her womb; and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.
She called out with a loud voice and said, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!
Why am I so favored, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
For behold, when the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the baby leaped in my womb for joy!
Blessed is she who believed, for there will be a fulfillment of the things which have been spoken to her from the Lord!”

lessons.title: Mary’s song of praise
lessons.subtitle: Mercy remembered across generations.
lessons.artworkAlt: A woman stands prayerfully above hillside homes and harvest fields in warm morning light.
lessons.summary: Mary praises God her Savior for noticing her humble situation. Her song celebrates God’s mercy, the lifting of the lowly, and food for the hungry. She remembers God’s help for Israel and the promise to Abraham.

challenge.prompt: Whose needs does Mary’s song especially notice?
challenge.explanation: Mary’s praise looks beyond herself. She celebrates God’s mercy toward the lowly and his faithfulness to earlier promises.

lessons.takeaway: Let gratitude open your eyes to people easily overlooked.
lessons.application: As you give thanks today, whose overlooked need could you also notice?

verses.text: Mary said, “My soul magnifies the Lord.
My spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior,
for he has looked at the humble state of his servant. For behold, from now on, all generations will call me blessed.
For he who is mighty has done great things for me. Holy is his name.
His mercy is for generations and generations on those who fear him.
He has shown strength with his arm. He has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts.
He has put down princes from their thrones, and has exalted the lowly.
He has filled the hungry with good things. He has sent the rich away empty.
He has given help to Israel, his servant, that he might remember mercy,
as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and his offspring forever.”
Mary stayed with her about three months, and then returned to her house.

lessons.title: His name is John
lessons.subtitle: A name followed by praise.
lessons.artworkAlt: An older father writes on a wax tablet beside a woman holding an infant, with neighbors gathered nearby.
lessons.summary: Elizabeth gives birth, and neighbors rejoice with her. When relatives propose naming the baby after his father, Elizabeth says John. Zacharias confirms the name on a writing tablet. His speech returns, and he begins blessing God.

challenge.prompt: Put these naming-day events in order.
challenge.explanation: Elizabeth names John first; Zacharias then confirms it. The restored speech leads directly to praise and the neighbors’ wonder.

lessons.takeaway: Received mercy can turn an ordinary gathering toward gratitude.
lessons.application: What recent kindness could you name with gratitude when you next meet someone?

verses.text: Now the time that Elizabeth should give birth was fulfilled, and she gave birth to a son.
Her neighbors and her relatives heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy toward her, and they rejoiced with her.
On the eighth day, they came to circumcise the child; and they would have called him Zacharias, after the name of his father.
His mother answered, “Not so; but he will be called John.”
They said to her, “There is no one among your relatives who is called by this name.”
They made signs to his father, what he would have him called.
He asked for a writing tablet, and wrote, “His name is John.” They all marveled.
His mouth was opened immediately and his tongue freed, and he spoke, blessing God.
Fear came on all who lived around them, and all these sayings were talked about throughout all the hill country of Judea.
All who heard them laid them up in their heart, saying, “What then will this child be?” The hand of the Lord was with him.

lessons.title: Born in Bethlehem
lessons.subtitle: A humble place to begin.
lessons.artworkAlt: A humble stone shelter holds a feeding trough with folded linen, warmed by soft light from its doorway.
lessons.summary: An enrollment brings Joseph and Mary from Nazareth to Bethlehem, David’s city. While they are there, Mary gives birth to her firstborn son. She wraps him in cloth and lays him in a feeding trough because the inn has no room.

challenge.prompt: Where does Mary lay her newborn son?
challenge.explanation: Luke places Jesus’ birth in humble circumstances. The feeding trough is part of the passage, rather than an added decoration.

lessons.takeaway: God’s story invites attention beyond impressive places and appearances.
lessons.application: What quiet or ordinary setting helps you make room to reflect on Jesus?

verses.text: Now in those days, a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be enrolled.
This was the first enrollment made when Quirinius was governor of Syria.
All went to enroll themselves, everyone to his own city.
Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judea, to David’s city, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David,
to enroll himself with Mary, who was pledged to be married to him as wife, being pregnant.
While they were there, the day had come for her to give birth.
She gave birth to her firstborn son. She wrapped him in bands of cloth and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no room for them in the inn.

lessons.title: Shepherds hear good news
lessons.subtitle: Wonder becomes witness.
lessons.artworkAlt: Shepherds watch a luminous night sky above their flock, with Bethlehem’s distant homes on the hillside.
lessons.summary: Shepherds watching their flock at night hear an angel announce the Savior’s birth. They hurry to Bethlehem and find the baby as described. They share what they heard, then return praising God for what they have seen.

challenge.prompt: Put the shepherds’ experience in order.
challenge.explanation: The shepherds move from hearing the announcement to seeing its sign. Their response includes sharing the news and praising God.

lessons.takeaway: Make space to notice, remember, and share good news.
lessons.application: What detail in this passage would you like to share with someone, in your own words?

verses.text: There were shepherds in the same country staying in the field, and keeping watch by night over their flock.
Behold, an angel of the Lord stood by them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were terrified.
The angel said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy which will be to all the people.
For there is born to you today, in David’s city, a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.
This is the sign to you: you will find a baby wrapped in strips of cloth, lying in a feeding trough.”
Suddenly, there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army praising God and saying,
“Glory to God in the highest, on earth peace, good will toward men.”
When the angels went away from them into the sky, the shepherds said to one another, “Let’s go to Bethlehem, now, and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.”
They came with haste and found both Mary and Joseph, and the baby was lying in the feeding trough.
When they saw it, they publicized widely the saying which was spoken to them about this child.
All who heard it wondered at the things which were spoken to them by the shepherds.
But Mary kept all these sayings, pondering them in her heart.
The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, just as it was told them.

lessons.title: Simeon and Anna
lessons.subtitle: Hope recognizes its fulfillment.
lessons.artworkAlt: An elderly man and woman stand beside tall temple columns in warm light, their faces filled with gratitude.
lessons.summary: Jesus’ parents bring him to the temple. Simeon receives the child and praises God for salvation prepared for all peoples. Anna, a prophetess devoted to worship, gives thanks and speaks about the child to others awaiting redemption.

challenge.prompt: What do Simeon and Anna both do?

choices.text: They respond with praise and thanks

challenge.explanation: Their long attention to God leads to recognition and gratitude. Both speak about the significance of the child before them.

lessons.takeaway: Patient hope can nurture attention, gratitude, and words of encouragement.
lessons.application: Who has modeled patient hope for you, and how might you thank them?

verses.text: When the days of their purification according to the law of Moses were fulfilled, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord
(as it is written in the law of the Lord, “Every male who opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord”),
and to offer a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the Lord, “A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.”
Behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon. This man was righteous and devout, looking for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was on him.
It had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he should not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.
He came in the Spirit into the temple. When the parents brought in the child, Jesus, that they might do concerning him according to the custom of the law,
then he received him into his arms and blessed God, and said,
“Now you are releasing your servant, Master, according to your word, in peace;
for my eyes have seen your salvation,
which you have prepared before the face of all peoples;
a light for revelation to the nations, and the glory of your people Israel.”
Joseph and his mother were marveling at the things which were spoken concerning him.
Simeon blessed them, and said to Mary, his mother, “Behold, this child is appointed for the falling and the rising of many in Israel, and for a sign which is spoken against.
Yes, a sword will pierce through your own soul, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”
There was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher (she was of a great age, having lived with a husband seven years from her virginity,
and she had been a widow for about eighty-four years), who didn’t depart from the temple, worshiping with fastings and petitions night and day.
Coming up at that very hour, she gave thanks to the Lord, and spoke of him to all those who were looking for redemption in Jerusalem.

lessons.title: Found in the temple
