lessons.subtitle: Listening and asking questions.
lessons.artworkAlt: Rolled scrolls rest beside seated teachers in a sunlit temple courtyard framed by stone columns.
lessons.summary: After Passover, Jesus’ parents discover he is missing from their traveling company. They return to Jerusalem and find him among the temple teachers, listening and asking questions. He then returns to Nazareth with them and continues to grow.

challenge.prompt: Put these events in order.

choices.text: His parents find him in the temple
He returns to Nazareth with them

challenge.explanation: Luke shows Jesus listening and questioning among teachers. The account ends with his return home, obedience, and continued growth.

lessons.takeaway: Listening and thoughtful questions belong in a life of learning.
lessons.application: What question could you explore thoughtfully the next time you read a Gospel passage?

verses.text: His parents went every year to Jerusalem at the feast of the Passover.
When he was twelve years old, they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast;
and when they had fulfilled the days, as they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. Joseph and his mother didn’t know it,
but supposing him to be in the company, they went a day’s journey; and they looked for him among their relatives and acquaintances.
When they didn’t find him, they returned to Jerusalem, looking for him.
After three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the middle of the teachers, both listening to them and asking them questions.
All who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers.
When they saw him, they were astonished; and his mother said to him, “Son, why have you treated us this way? Behold, your father and I were anxiously looking for you.”
He said to them, “Why were you looking for me? Didn’t you know that I must be in my Father’s house?”
They didn’t understand the saying which he spoke to them.
And he went down with them and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them, and his mother kept all these sayings in her heart.
And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men.

lessons.title: Good news in Nazareth
lessons.subtitle: A promise read aloud.
lessons.artworkAlt: A closed scroll rests on a wooden reading stand inside a sunlit stone synagogue.
lessons.summary: In Nazareth’s synagogue, Jesus reads Isaiah’s words about good news, freedom, and restoration. He announces their fulfillment in his listeners’ hearing. When he recalls God’s care for people beyond Israel, the gathering becomes angry, but he leaves safely.

challenge.prompt: What does Jesus announce after reading Isaiah?

choices.text: The Scripture is fulfilled in their hearing

challenge.explanation: Jesus connects Isaiah’s promise to his own mission. The account also challenges the listeners’ expectation that hometown ties guarantee privilege.

lessons.takeaway: Attend to Jesus’ mission, including people beyond your familiar circle.
lessons.application: Who outside your familiar circle might you listen to or treat with greater care?

verses.text: He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. He entered, as was his custom, into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and stood up to read.
The book of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him. He opened the book, and found the place where it was written,

“The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent me to heal the broken hearted, to proclaim release to the captives, recovering of sight to the blind, to deliver those who are crushed,
and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.”
He closed the book, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down. The eyes of all in the synagogue were fastened on him.
He began to tell them, “Today, this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”
All testified about him and wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth; and they said, “Isn’t this Joseph’s son?”
He said to them, “Doubtless you will tell me this proverb, ‘Physician, heal yourself! Whatever we have heard done at Capernaum, do also here in your hometown.’ ”
He said, “Most certainly I tell you, no prophet is acceptable in his hometown.
But truly I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the sky was shut up three years and six months, when a great famine came over all the land.
Elijah was sent to none of them, except to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow.
There were many lepers in Israel in the time of Elisha the prophet, yet not one of them was cleansed, except Naaman, the Syrian.”
They were all filled with wrath in the synagogue as they heard these things.
They rose up, threw him out of the city, and led him to the brow of the hill that their city was built on, that they might throw him off the cliff.
But he, passing through the middle of them, went his way.

lessons.title: A catch and a calling
lessons.subtitle: The boats return; a journey begins.
lessons.artworkAlt: Two wooden fishing boats sit low in the water beside heavy nets of fish at a bright lakeshore.
lessons.summary: After teaching from Simon’s boat, Jesus tells him to lower the nets. Despite an empty night’s work, Simon does so, and the catch fills two boats. Jesus reassures the astonished fishermen, who bring the boats ashore and follow him.

challenge.prompt: Put the fishermen’s actions in order.
challenge.explanation: The large catch leads into a calling to follow Jesus. The story’s destination is discipleship, beyond an unusually successful fishing trip.

lessons.takeaway: Consider what following Jesus asks of your ordinary daily work.
lessons.application: Which teaching of Jesus could shape a choice in your work or responsibilities today?

verses.text: Now while the multitude pressed on him and heard the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret.
He saw two boats standing by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets.
He entered into one of the boats, which was Simon’s, and asked him to put out a little from the land. He sat down and taught the multitudes from the boat.
When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, “Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.”
Simon answered him, “Master, we worked all night and caught nothing; but at your word I will let down the net.”
When they had done this, they caught a great multitude of fish, and their net was breaking.
They beckoned to their partners in the other boat, that they should come and help them. They came and filled both boats, so that they began to sink.
But Simon Peter, when he saw it, fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.”
For he was amazed, and all who were with him, at the catch of fish which they had caught;
and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. Jesus said to Simon, “Don’t be afraid. From now on you will be catching people alive.”
When they had brought their boats to land, they left everything, and followed him.

lessons.title: Compassion at Nain
lessons.subtitle: Grief is met with compassion.
lessons.artworkAlt: A mother embraces her living adult son at a stone town gate, while nearby people look on with relief.
lessons.summary: At Nain’s gate, Jesus meets a funeral procession for a widow’s only son. He sees her grief and has compassion. At his command, the young man sits up and speaks, and Jesus gives him back to his mother.

challenge.prompt: What moves Jesus when he sees the widow?

choices.text: The crowd’s request for a sign

challenge.explanation: Luke highlights Jesus’ compassion before describing the miracle. The gathered people respond by glorifying God and recognizing his care.

lessons.takeaway: Let another person’s grief call forth presence and compassionate care.
lessons.application: Who might appreciate a quiet message of care or practical help during a difficult time?

verses.text: Soon afterwards, he went to a city called Nain. Many of his disciples, along with a great multitude, went with him.
Now when he came near to the gate of the city, behold, one who was dead was carried out, the only born son of his mother, and she was a widow. Many people of the city were with her.
When the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, “Don’t cry.”
He came near and touched the coffin, and the bearers stood still. He said, “Young man, I tell you, arise!”
He who was dead sat up and began to speak. Then he gave him to his mother.
Fear took hold of all, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and, “God has visited his people!”
This report went out concerning him in the whole of Judea and in all the surrounding region.

lessons.title: John’s honest question
lessons.subtitle: Look at what is heard and seen.
lessons.artworkAlt: Two travelers walk along a village road toward welcoming homes, carrying the posture of attentive messengers.
lessons.summary: John sends two disciples to ask whether Jesus is the expected one. Jesus has been healing people and bringing good news. He tells the messengers to report what they have seen and heard, including good news reaching the poor.

challenge.prompt: What does Jesus tell the messengers to report?

choices.text: What they have seen and heard

challenge.explanation: Jesus responds to John’s question with the works and message before the visitors. His answer gives them something concrete to report.

lessons.takeaway: Bring honest questions and attend carefully to the Gospel’s testimony.
lessons.application: Which detail about Jesus in this passage would you like to understand more deeply?

verses.text: The disciples of John told him about all these things.
John, calling to himself two of his disciples, sent them to Jesus, saying, “Are you the one who is coming, or should we look for another?”
When the men had come to him, they said, “John the Baptizer has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you he who comes, or should we look for another?’ ”
In that hour he cured many of diseases and plagues and evil spirits; and to many who were blind he gave sight.

Jesus answered them, “Go and tell John the things which you have seen and heard: that the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them.
Blessed is he who finds no occasion for stumbling in me.”

lessons.title: Forgiven and at peace
lessons.subtitle: Mercy awakens love.
lessons.artworkAlt: An alabaster perfume jar and soft cloth sit beside a low dining table in a warmly lit room.
lessons.summary: A woman weeps at Jesus’ feet and anoints them during a meal. Simon questions her presence. Jesus explains that greater forgiven debt awakens greater love, then assures the woman of forgiveness and sends her away in peace.

challenge.prompt: In Jesus’ illustration, which debtor is expected to love more?
challenge.explanation: The debtors’ story helps Simon notice the woman’s love in relation to forgiveness. Jesus ends by addressing her with peace.

lessons.takeaway: Remembering received forgiveness can deepen gratitude and love for others.
lessons.application: How might remembering kindness you have received change your response to someone today?

verses.text: One of the Pharisees invited him to eat with him. He entered into the Pharisee’s house and sat at the table.
Behold, a woman in the city who was a sinner, when she knew that he was reclining in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster jar of ointment.
Standing behind at his feet weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears, and she wiped them with the hair of her head, kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment.
Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw it, he said to himself, “This man, if he were a prophet, would have perceived who and what kind of woman this is who touches him, that she is a sinner.”
Jesus answered him, “Simon, I have something to tell you.” He said, “Teacher, say on.”
“A certain lender had two debtors. The one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty.
When they couldn’t pay, he forgave them both. Which of them therefore will love him most?”
Simon answered, “He, I suppose, to whom he forgave the most.” He said to him, “You have judged correctly.”

Turning to the woman, he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I entered into your house, and you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears, and wiped them with the hair of her head.
You gave me no kiss, but she, since the time I came in, has not ceased to kiss my feet.
You didn’t anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.
Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But one to whom little is forgiven, loves little.”
He said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.”
Those who sat at the table with him began to say to themselves, “Who is this who even forgives sins?”
He said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you. Go in peace.”

lessons.title: Women who supported the work
lessons.subtitle: Resources placed in service.
lessons.artworkAlt: Three women carrying baskets of provisions walk together along a sunlit road between village homes.
lessons.summary: Jesus travels through cities and villages announcing God’s kingdom. The Twelve accompany him, along with women who have received healing. Luke names Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Susanna among those supporting the group from their own resources.

challenge.prompt: How do these women support the group?

choices.text: By asking the Twelve for supplies

challenge.explanation: Luke names women as active participants in this traveling ministry. Their practical support helps sustain the work of sharing good news.

lessons.takeaway: Practical generosity can support meaningful work and the people doing it.
lessons.application: What resource—time, skill, or something material—could you share to support a worthwhile need?

verses.text: Soon afterwards, he went about through cities and villages, preaching and bringing the good news of God’s Kingdom. With him were the twelve,
and certain women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary who was called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out;
and Joanna, the wife of Chuzas, Herod’s steward; Susanna; and many others who served them from their possessions.

lessons.title: Sent two by two
lessons.subtitle: Peace arrives before the message.
lessons.artworkAlt: Two travelers approach an open doorway in a stone village, where a host waits to receive them.
lessons.summary: Jesus appoints seventy others and sends them ahead in pairs. He asks them to pray for workers and enter homes with a greeting of peace. They are to receive hospitality and announce that God’s kingdom has come near.

challenge.prompt: What should they first say when entering a house?

choices.text: News that the kingdom is near

challenge.explanation: The instructions begin each household visit with peace. Jesus sends these messengers to depend on hospitality while announcing God’s kingdom.

lessons.takeaway: Let a peaceful approach shape how you enter another’s space.
lessons.application: What could help you bring a peaceful attitude into your next conversation?

verses.text: Now after these things, the Lord also appointed seventy others, and sent them two by two ahead of him into every city and place where he was about to come.
Then he said to them, “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore to the Lord of the harvest, that he may send out laborers into his harvest.
Go your ways. Behold, I send you out as lambs among wolves.
Carry no purse, nor wallet, nor sandals. Greet no one on the way.
Into whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house.’
If a son of peace is there, your peace will rest on him; but if not, it will return to you.
Remain in that same house, eating and drinking the things they give, for the laborer is worthy of his wages. Don’t go from house to house.
Into whatever city you enter and they receive you, eat the things that are set before you.
Heal the sick who are there and tell them, ‘God’s Kingdom has come near to you.’
But into whatever city you enter and they don’t receive you, go out into its streets and say,
‘Even the dust from your city that clings to us, we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that God’s Kingdom has come near to you.’
I tell you, it will be more tolerable in that day for Sodom than for that city.

lessons.title: Mary and Martha
lessons.subtitle: Make room to listen.
lessons.artworkAlt: One woman sits attentively on cushions while another stands beside bread and dishes in a sunlit home.
lessons.summary: Martha welcomes Jesus into her home while Mary sits and listens to his word. Distracted by much serving, Martha asks him to intervene. Jesus addresses her anxiety and says Mary has chosen the good part, which will remain hers.

challenge.prompt: What is Mary doing when Martha speaks?
challenge.explanation: Jesus draws attention to Martha’s anxiety and Mary’s listening. The passage invites attention to his word amid competing demands.

lessons.takeaway: Allow attentive listening a place among your responsibilities and service.
lessons.application: Where could you make a small, unhurried space to listen to Scripture today?

verses.text: As they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house.
She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet and heard his word.
But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.”
Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

lessons.title: A friend at midnight
lessons.subtitle: Keep bringing your needs to God.
lessons.artworkAlt: A person with an empty basket knocks at a friend’s lamplit doorway under a midnight sky.
lessons.summary: Jesus tells of a person asking a friend for bread at midnight to feed a visitor. Persistence brings help. He then encourages asking, seeking, and knocking, and points to the heavenly Father’s generosity in giving the Holy Spirit.

challenge.prompt: What gift does Jesus name at the passage’s end?
challenge.explanation: The bread request leads to teaching about prayer. Jesus names the Holy Spirit when describing the Father’s generous response.

lessons.takeaway: Keep praying with trust in the Father’s generosity and care.
lessons.application: What need or concern would you like to bring honestly to God in prayer?

verses.text: He said to them, “Which of you, if you go to a friend at midnight and tell him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves of bread,
for a friend of mine has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him,’
and he from within will answer and say, ‘Don’t bother me. The door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I can’t get up and give it to you’?
I tell you, although he will not rise and give it to him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence, he will get up and give him as many as he needs.
“I tell you, keep asking, and it will be given you. Keep seeking, and you will find. Keep knocking, and it will be opened to you.
For everyone who asks receives. He who seeks finds. To him who knocks it will be opened.
“Which of you fathers, if your son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, he won’t give him a snake instead of a fish, will he?
Or if he asks for an egg, he won’t give him a scorpion, will he?
If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?”

lessons.title: Hearing and keeping
lessons.subtitle: A blessing linked with response.
lessons.artworkAlt: A nearly closed parchment scroll lies beside leather sandals at a sunlit stone doorway.
lessons.summary: As Jesus speaks, a woman in the crowd praises the mother who bore and nursed him. Jesus redirects attention to those who hear God’s word and keep it, connecting blessing with a response to what God says.

challenge.prompt: Whom does Jesus call blessed in his response?

choices.text: Those related to him by birth
Those who hear and keep God’s word

challenge.explanation: Jesus shifts attention from a family connection to hearing and keeping God’s word. His response invites the whole crowd to listen.

lessons.takeaway: Let what you hear in Scripture shape a practical response.
lessons.application: Which word or teaching from today’s reading could influence one choice you make?

verses.text: It came to pass, as he said these things, a certain woman out of the multitude lifted up her voice and said to him, “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts which nursed you!”
But he said, “On the contrary, blessed are those who hear the word of God, and keep it.”

lessons.title: Keep your lamp burning
lessons.subtitle: Readiness expressed in faithful attention.
lessons.artworkAlt: A glowing oil lamp stands beside a closed doorway while blue twilight settles outside.
lessons.summary: Jesus pictures servants keeping their lamps burning, ready to open when their master returns. He describes the master honoring watchful servants by serving them. Jesus then calls his listeners to readiness because the Son of Man’s arrival is unexpected.

challenge.prompt: What are the servants prepared to do?

choices.text: Open promptly when their master returns

challenge.explanation: The servants’ readiness is practical and attentive. Jesus emphasizes being prepared for his coming without providing a timetable to calculate.

lessons.takeaway: Practice faithful attention today without trying to predict God’s timing.
lessons.application: What ordinary responsibility could you approach with greater care and faithfulness today?

verses.text: “Let your waist be dressed and your lamps burning.
Be like men watching for their lord when he returns from the wedding feast, that when he comes and knocks, they may immediately open to him.
Blessed are those servants whom the lord will find watching when he comes. Most certainly I tell you that he will dress himself, make them recline, and will come and serve them.
They will be blessed if he comes in the second or third watch and finds them so.
But know this, that if the master of the house had known in what hour the thief was coming, he would have watched and not allowed his house to be broken into.
Therefore be ready also, for the Son of Man is coming in an hour that you don’t expect him.”

lessons.title: Another year for the fig tree
lessons.subtitle: Patience makes room for a response.
lessons.artworkAlt: A gardener loosens soil around a leafy, fruitless fig tree, with a basket of compost nearby.
lessons.summary: A vineyard owner looks for figs and finds none. He tells the gardener to remove the unfruitful tree. The gardener asks for another year to dig around it and add fertilizer, allowing more time for fruit to grow.

challenge.prompt: What does the gardener request?

choices.text: Another year to tend the tree
A different place to plant it

challenge.explanation: The gardener’s request joins patience with active care. The parable leaves open whether the extra opportunity will produce fruit.

lessons.takeaway: Receive an opportunity to change with patience and purposeful action.
lessons.application: What small practice could you tend patiently as you respond to Jesus’ teaching?

verses.text: He spoke this parable. “A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none.
He said to the vine dresser, ‘Behold, these three years I have come looking for fruit on this fig tree, and found none. Cut it down! Why does it waste the soil?’
He answered, ‘Lord, leave it alone this year also, until I dig around it and fertilize it.
If it bears fruit, fine; but if not, after that, you can cut it down.’ ”

lessons.title: A woman stands tall
lessons.subtitle: Her dignity is brought into view.
lessons.artworkAlt: A woman stands upright with thankful, raised hands inside a synagogue, warmly lit between stone columns.
lessons.summary: Jesus frees a woman who has been bent over for eighteen years. She stands straight and praises God. When the synagogue ruler objects to Sabbath healing, Jesus calls her a daughter of Abraham and defends her release.

challenge.prompt: How does Jesus describe the woman when defending her?

choices.text: As a visitor from another town
As a member of the ruler’s family

challenge.explanation: Jesus names her belonging as a daughter of Abraham. He argues that her release is fitting on the Sabbath.

lessons.takeaway: Notice the dignity and belonging of people others might overlook.
lessons.application: How could you make a shared space more welcoming to someone who is often overlooked?

verses.text: He was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath day.
Behold, there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity eighteen years. She was bent over and could in no way straighten herself up.
When Jesus saw her, he called her and said to her, “Woman, you are freed from your infirmity.”
He laid his hands on her, and immediately she stood up straight and glorified God.

The ruler of the synagogue, being indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the multitude, “There are six days in which men ought to work. Therefore come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day!”
Therefore the Lord answered him, “You hypocrites! Doesn’t each one of you free his ox or his donkey from the stall on the Sabbath and lead him away to water?
Ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound eighteen long years, be freed from this bondage on the Sabbath day?”
As he said these things, all his adversaries were disappointed; and all the multitude rejoiced for all the glorious things that were done by him.

lessons.title: Room at the table
lessons.subtitle: Welcome without calculating a return.
lessons.artworkAlt: A simple feast table holds bread and fruit, with open seats arranged to welcome people into a courtyard.
lessons.summary: Watching guests choose honored places, Jesus teaches humility at a feast. He also tells the host to welcome people who cannot repay the invitation. Both instructions challenge meals organized around status, advantage, and getting something back.

challenge.prompt: Whom does Jesus especially tell the host to invite?

choices.text: Friends who will invite him back
People unable to return the favor

challenge.explanation: Jesus challenges both grasping for honor and hospitality as an exchange. His invitation makes room for people without social advantage.

lessons.takeaway: Offer welcome without making repayment or status the condition.
lessons.application: Who could you include in a meal, conversation, or gathering without expecting anything in return?

verses.text: He spoke a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the best seats, and said to them,
“When you are invited by anyone to a wedding feast, don’t sit in the best seat, since perhaps someone more honorable than you might be invited by him,
and he who invited both of you would come and tell you, ‘Make room for this person.’ Then you would begin, with shame, to take the lowest place.

But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when he who invited you comes, he may tell you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at the table with you.
For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

He also said to the one who had invited him, “When you make a dinner or a supper, don’t call your friends, nor your brothers, nor your kinsmen, nor rich neighbors, or perhaps they might also return the favor, and pay you back.
But when you make a feast, ask the poor, the maimed, the lame, or the blind;
and you will be blessed, because they don’t have the resources to repay you. For you will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous.”

lessons.title: The great banquet
lessons.subtitle: The invitation reaches farther.
lessons.artworkAlt: A servant welcomes a varied group of adults from the street into a courtyard prepared for a generous banquet.
lessons.summary: In Jesus’ parable, invited guests make excuses when a banquet is ready. The host sends his servant into the city to bring people usually overlooked. When places remain, the invitation reaches the roads beyond, filling the house.

challenge.prompt: What does the host do after hearing the excuses?

choices.text: Sends the servant to invite others

challenge.explanation: The first guests refuse a ready invitation. The host then extends welcome beyond them, including people without the same social standing.

lessons.takeaway: Consider how you respond to an invitation that interrupts convenience.
lessons.application: What worthwhile invitation might you be dismissing because it disrupts your usual routine?

verses.text: When one of those who sat at the table with him heard these things, he said to him, “Blessed is he who will feast in God’s Kingdom!”
But he said to him, “A certain man made a great supper, and he invited many people.
He sent out his servant at supper time to tell those who were invited, ‘Come, for everything is ready now.’
They all as one began to make excuses. “The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go and see it. Please have me excused.’
“Another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I must go try them out. Please have me excused.’
“Another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I can’t come.’

“That servant came, and told his lord these things. Then the master of the house, being angry, said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor, maimed, blind, and lame.’
“The servant said, ‘Lord, it is done as you commanded, and there is still room.’
“The lord said to the servant, ‘Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.
For I tell you that none of those men who were invited will taste of my supper. For many are called, but few are chosen.’ ”

lessons.title: Count the cost
lessons.subtitle: Following with an honest understanding.
lessons.artworkAlt: A builder studies a measuring cord beside a partly built stone tower and carefully arranged building stones.
lessons.summary: Jesus tells the crowds that following him is costly. He pictures a builder calculating whether a tower can be completed and a king considering a battle. These examples ask listeners to face the commitment of discipleship honestly.

challenge.prompt: What does the builder do before beginning the tower?

choices.text: Calls workers to lay the foundation
Calculates whether the resources are enough

challenge.explanation: The builder’s calculation illustrates serious commitment. Jesus uses it while speaking about the demands of following him, including possessions and loyalties.

lessons.takeaway: Take Jesus’ call seriously and consider your commitments with honesty.
lessons.application: Which commitment or possession might you need to reconsider as you follow Jesus’ teaching?

verses.text: Now great multitudes were going with him. He turned and said to them,
“If anyone comes to me, and doesn’t disregard his own father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters, yes, and his own life also, he can’t be my disciple.
Whoever doesn’t bear his own cross and come after me, can’t be my disciple.
For which of you, desiring to build a tower, doesn’t first sit down and count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it?
Or perhaps, when he has laid a foundation and isn’t able to finish, everyone who sees begins to mock him,
saying, ‘This man began to build and wasn’t able to finish.’
Or what king, as he goes to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and consider whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand?
Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends an envoy and asks for conditions of peace.
So therefore, whoever of you who doesn’t renounce all that he has, he can’t be my disciple.

lessons.title: The lost coin
lessons.subtitle: A careful search ends in joy.
lessons.artworkAlt: A woman with a broom and a glowing lamp discovers a small coin on the floor of her home.
lessons.summary: Jesus describes a woman who loses one of her ten coins. She lights a lamp, sweeps, and searches carefully until she finds it. She then invites friends and neighbors to rejoice, illustrating heaven’s joy over a sinner’s repentance.

challenge.prompt: Put the woman’s response in order.

choices.text: She lights a lamp and searches

challenge.explanation: The search leads to finding and shared celebration. Jesus explicitly connects that rejoicing with joy over one sinner who repents.

lessons.takeaway: Leave room for joy when someone turns toward God.
lessons.application: How might you welcome another person’s positive change with encouragement rather than suspicion?

verses.text: “Or what woman, if she had ten drachma coins, if she lost one drachma coin, wouldn’t light a lamp, sweep the house, and seek diligently until she found it?
When she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the drachma which I had lost!’
Even so, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner repenting.”

lessons.title: The father welcomes his son
lessons.subtitle: Compassion runs toward a returning child.
lessons.artworkAlt: A father embraces his travel-worn adult son at the entrance to their home, with warm light behind them.
lessons.summary: A younger son wastes his inheritance and returns home in need. His father runs to welcome him and calls for a celebration. The older son objects, and the father invites him to share the joy of his brother’s return.

challenge.prompt: Put the younger son’s story in order.

choices.text: He leaves and spends his inheritance

challenge.explanation: The father responds to the returning son with compassion. His later appeal also invites the older son into that joy.

lessons.takeaway: Received mercy invites both a return and a generous welcome.
lessons.application: Is there a positive change in someone else’s life that you could celebrate rather than resent?

verses.text: He said, “A certain man had two sons.
The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me my share of your property.’ So he divided his livelihood between them.
Not many days after, the younger son gathered all of this together and traveled into a far country. There he wasted his property with riotous living.
When he had spent all of it, there arose a severe famine in that country, and he began to be in need.
He went and joined himself to one of the citizens of that country, and he sent him into his fields to feed pigs.
He wanted to fill his belly with the pods that the pigs ate, but no one gave him any.
But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough to spare, and I’m dying with hunger!
I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight.
I am no more worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.” ’
“He arose and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.
The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
“But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring out the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet.
Bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let’s eat and celebrate;
for this, my son, was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found.’ Then they began to celebrate.
“Now his elder son was in the field. As he came near to the house, he heard music and dancing.
He called one of the servants to him and asked what was going on.
He said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and healthy.’
But he was angry and would not go in. Therefore his father came out and begged him.
But he answered his father, ‘Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours, but you never gave me a goat, that I might celebrate with my friends.
But when this your son came, who has devoured your living with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him.’
“He said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.
But it was appropriate to celebrate and be glad, for this, your brother, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.’ ”

lessons.title: Lazarus at the gate
lessons.subtitle: A warning about overlooked need.
lessons.artworkAlt: A poor man sits respectfully portrayed beside a wealthy household’s gate, with a small bowl near him.
lessons.summary: Jesus tells of a rich man living luxuriously while Lazarus suffers at his gate. After death, their situations reverse. The rich man asks for a warning to his brothers, but Abraham directs them to Moses and the prophets.

challenge.prompt: What does Abraham say the brothers should listen to?

choices.text: A messenger returned from the dead
A new warning from their brother

challenge.explanation: The story joins neglected need with a call to heed Scripture. A dramatic sign cannot substitute for listening to God’s instruction.

lessons.takeaway: Let Scripture move you to notice needs near your door.
lessons.application: What nearby need might you have learned to overlook, and what modest response is possible?

verses.text: “Now there was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, living in luxury every day.
A certain beggar, named Lazarus, was taken to his gate, full of sores,
and desiring to be fed with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table. Yes, even the dogs came and licked his sores.
The beggar died, and he was carried away by the angels to Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried.
In Hades, he lifted up his eyes, being in torment, and saw Abraham far off, and Lazarus at his bosom.
He cried and said, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue! For I am in anguish in this flame.’
“But Abraham said, ‘Son, remember that you, in your lifetime, received your good things, and Lazarus, in the same way, bad things. But here he is now comforted and you are in anguish.
Besides all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed, that those who want to pass from here to you are not able, and that no one may cross over from there to us.’
“He said, ‘I ask you therefore, father, that you would send him to my father’s house—
for I have five brothers—that he may testify to them, so they won’t also come into this place of torment.’
“But Abraham said to him, ‘They have Moses and the prophets. Let them listen to them.’
“He said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if one goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’
“He said to him, ‘If they don’t listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded if one rises from the dead.’ ”

lessons.title: One returned to give thanks
lessons.subtitle: Gratitude turns back.
lessons.artworkAlt: A grateful man kneels alone on a sunlit village road, lifting his open hands toward the sky.
lessons.summary: Ten men with leprosy call to Jesus for mercy. He sends them to show themselves to the priests, and they are cleansed on the way. One returns praising God and thanking Jesus. Luke identifies this grateful man as a Samaritan.

challenge.prompt: Put these events in order.

choices.text: They are cleansed as they go

challenge.explanation: All ten receive cleansing, and one returns with gratitude. Jesus draws attention to the Samaritan’s response of praise and thanks.

lessons.takeaway: Let received kindness become a reason to pause and give thanks.
lessons.application: What kindness have you received that deserves a specific expression of thanks?

verses.text: As he was on his way to Jerusalem, he was passing along the borders of Samaria and Galilee.
As he entered into a certain village, ten men who were lepers met him, who stood at a distance.
They lifted up their voices, saying, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!”
When he saw them, he said to them, “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” As they went, they were cleansed.
One of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice.
He fell on his face at Jesus’ feet, giving him thanks; and he was a Samaritan.
Jesus answered, “Weren’t the ten cleansed? But where are the nine?
Were there none found who returned to give glory to God, except this foreigner?”
Then he said to him, “Get up, and go your way. Your faith has healed you.”

lessons.title: The persistent widow
lessons.subtitle: Keep praying without giving up.
lessons.artworkAlt: A determined older woman petitions a seated judge in a stone city court, her open hands emphasizing her request.
lessons.summary: Jesus tells of a widow who repeatedly asks an unjust judge to defend her. Though he initially refuses, her persistence leads him to act. Jesus contrasts this judge with God and encourages his listeners to keep praying.

challenge.prompt: Why does Luke say Jesus tells this parable?

choices.text: To encourage prayer without giving up
To teach that one request is enough

challenge.explanation: The unjust judge eventually responds despite his indifference. Jesus uses the contrast to encourage persistent prayer and confidence in God’s justice.

lessons.takeaway: Keep bringing your longing for justice to God in prayer.
lessons.application: What situation needing justice could you keep praying about while also seeking appropriate help?

verses.text: He also spoke a parable to them that they must always pray and not give up,
saying, “There was a judge in a certain city who didn’t fear God and didn’t respect man.
A widow was in that city, and she often came to him, saying, ‘Defend me from my adversary!’
He wouldn’t for a while; but afterward he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God nor respect man,
yet because this widow bothers me, I will defend her, or else she will wear me out by her continual coming.’ ”
The Lord said, “Listen to what the unrighteous judge says.
Won’t God avenge his chosen ones who are crying out to him day and night, and yet he exercises patience with them?
I tell you that he will avenge them quickly. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?”

lessons.title: Two men at prayer
lessons.subtitle: Mercy without comparison.
lessons.artworkAlt: Two men stand separately in a temple courtyard, one with his head bowed and his hands near his chest.
lessons.summary: Jesus tells of two men praying in the temple. One praises his own conduct while looking down on others. The tax collector stands apart and asks God for mercy. Jesus says the tax collector goes home justified rather than the other.

challenge.prompt: What does the tax collector ask God for?

choices.text: A higher standing than the other man
Mercy for himself as a sinner

challenge.explanation: Jesus addresses confidence in personal righteousness that despises others. The tax collector brings an honest plea for mercy instead of comparison.

lessons.takeaway: Approach God with honesty rather than measuring yourself against others.
lessons.application: What might change in your prayer if you set comparison with other people aside?

verses.text: He also spoke this parable to certain people who were convinced of their own righteousness, and who despised all others:
“Two men went up into the temple to pray; one was a Pharisee, and the other was a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood and prayed by himself like this: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men: extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.
I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all that I get.’
But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his chest, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”

lessons.title: Zacchaeus comes down
lessons.subtitle: A welcome and a concrete response.
lessons.artworkAlt: An adult man climbs down a leafy sycamore beside a busy stone-lined road through Jericho.
lessons.summary: Zacchaeus climbs a tree to see Jesus. Jesus calls him down and chooses to stay at his house. Zacchaeus welcomes him joyfully and speaks of generosity to the poor and repayment for wrongdoing. Jesus announces salvation.

challenge.prompt: Put these events in order.

choices.text: He speaks of giving and repayment

challenge.explanation: After welcoming Jesus, Zacchaeus describes concrete generosity and restitution. Jesus announces salvation and his mission to seek and save the lost.

lessons.takeaway: Consider how a changed heart can lead to concrete repair.
lessons.application: Is there an ordinary wrong you could begin to repair through an honest, practical step?

verses.text: He entered and was passing through Jericho.
There was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector, and he was rich.
He was trying to see who Jesus was, and couldn’t because of the crowd, because he was short.
He ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was going to pass that way.
When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and saw him, and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.”
He hurried, came down, and received him joyfully.
When they saw it, they all murmured, saying, “He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner.”
Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.”
Jesus said to him, “Today, salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham.
For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.”

lessons.title: Compassion and a touch
lessons.subtitle: A person is more than an illness.
lessons.artworkAlt: A man in clean linen kneels alone beside a sunlit village doorway with hands raised in gratitude.
lessons.summary: A man with leprosy kneels before Jesus and asks to be made clean. Moved with compassion, Jesus touches and heals him. He then sends the man to the priest, with instructions to make the offering Moses commanded.

challenge.prompt: What moves Jesus to reach toward the man?
challenge.explanation: Mark names compassion before the touch. The man receives personal care, not avoidance or a demand for payment.

lessons.takeaway: Compassion begins by seeing the person before the label.
lessons.application: Who might you listen to more carefully instead of making an assumption about their circumstances?

verses.text: A leper came to him, begging him, kneeling down to him, and saying to him, “If you want to, you can make me clean.”
Being moved with compassion, he stretched out his hand, and touched him, and said to him, “I want to. Be made clean.”
When he had said this, immediately the leprosy departed from him and he was made clean.
He strictly warned him and immediately sent him out,
and said to him, “See that you say nothing to anybody, but go show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing the things which Moses commanded, for a testimony to them.”

But he went out, and began to proclaim it much, and to spread about the matter, so that Jesus could no more openly enter into a city, but was outside in desert places. People came to him from everywhere.

lessons.title: Friends open a roof
lessons.subtitle: Care finds a way through.
lessons.artworkAlt: Four adults carefully lower a woven mat through an opening in the flat roof of a stone house.
lessons.summary: A crowd blocks four people carrying a paralyzed man to Jesus. They open the roof and lower his mat. Jesus forgives the man’s sins and, showing his authority to forgive, tells him to rise and go home.

challenge.prompt: Put these events in order.

choices.text: The man carries his mat home
Friends lower the mat through the roof

challenge.explanation: The friends bring him to Jesus. Forgiveness comes before the command to rise, revealing more than physical healing.

lessons.takeaway: Practical care can help someone reach support they need.
lessons.application: What barrier could you help remove for someone seeking support?

verses.text: When he entered again into Capernaum after some days, it was heard that he was at home.
Immediately many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even around the door; and he spoke the word to them.
Four people came, carrying a paralytic to him.
When they could not come near to him for the crowd, they removed the roof where he was. When they had broken it up, they let down the mat that the paralytic was lying on.
Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven you.”
But there were some of the scribes sitting there and reasoning in their hearts,
“Why does this man speak blasphemies like that? Who can forgive sins but God alone?”
Immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they so reasoned within themselves, said to them, “Why do you reason these things in your hearts?
Which is easier, to tell the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven;’ or to say, ‘Arise, and take up your bed, and walk’?
But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the paralytic—
“I tell you, arise, take up your mat, and go to your house.”
He arose, and immediately took up the mat and went out in front of them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying, “We never saw anything like this!”

lessons.title: Levi leaves the table
lessons.subtitle: An invitation reaches the overlooked.
lessons.artworkAlt: A tax collector leaves a small wooden counting table beside a lakeside road.
lessons.summary: Jesus calls Levi from his tax office, and Levi follows. Later he eats with tax collectors and sinners. When challenged, Jesus compares his mission to a physician’s work and says he came to call sinners to repentance.

challenge.prompt: How does Jesus describe his mission?
challenge.explanation: Jesus explains his welcome through the image of a physician. His call offers relationship and an invitation to change.

lessons.takeaway: Welcome can open a door toward a changed life.
lessons.application: Who could you welcome without reducing them to their past?

verses.text: He went out again by the seaside. All the multitude came to him, and he taught them.
As he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax office. He said to him, “Follow me.” And he arose and followed him.
He was reclining at the table in his house, and many tax collectors and sinners sat down with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many, and they followed him.
The scribes and the Pharisees, when they saw that he was eating with the sinners and tax collectors, said to his disciples, “Why is it that he eats and drinks with tax collectors and sinners?”
When Jesus heard it, he said to them, “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”

lessons.title: A gift of rest
lessons.subtitle: Notice the purpose behind the practice.
lessons.artworkAlt: Three men walk along a sunlit grain field, with the nearest man picking ripe heads of grain.
lessons.summary: As the disciples pick grain on the Sabbath, some Pharisees object. Jesus recalls David feeding hungry companions. He says the Sabbath was made for people and declares that the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.

challenge.prompt: What does Jesus say about the Sabbath?

choices.text: People were made for the Sabbath

challenge.explanation: Jesus answers the objection by recalling human need and the Sabbath’s purpose, while affirming his own authority over it.

lessons.takeaway: Rest invites us to consider people and their needs.
lessons.application: How could your next period of rest make room for someone’s needs as well as your own?

verses.text: He was going on the Sabbath day through the grain fields; and his disciples began, as they went, to pluck the ears of grain.
The Pharisees said to him, “Behold, why do they do that which is not lawful on the Sabbath day?”
He said to them, “Did you never read what David did when he had need and was hungry—he, and those who were with him?
How he entered into God’s house at the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the show bread, which is not lawful to eat except for the priests, and gave also to those who were with him?”
He said to them, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.
Therefore the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.”

lessons.title: Doing good on the Sabbath
lessons.subtitle: Mercy belongs in the room.
lessons.artworkAlt: A man holds his restored hand open in wonder inside a modest stone synagogue.
lessons.summary: In a synagogue, a man has a withered hand. Some watch Jesus for a reason to accuse him. Jesus asks whether the Sabbath permits doing good or harm. He restores the man’s hand, while his opponents begin plotting against him.

challenge.prompt: What contrast does Jesus put before his listeners?
challenge.explanation: Jesus centers the question on doing good. The restored hand exposes the hardness of people seeking an accusation.

lessons.takeaway: Another person’s need deserves attention, even when it interrupts.
lessons.application: Where might protecting your routine be keeping you from a simple act of care?

verses.text: He entered again into the synagogue, and there was a man there whose hand was withered.
They watched him, whether he would heal him on the Sabbath day, that they might accuse him.
He said to the man whose hand was withered, “Stand up.”
He said to them, “Is it lawful on the Sabbath day to do good or to do harm? To save a life or to kill?” But they were silent.

When he had looked around at them with anger, being grieved at the hardening of their hearts, he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and his hand was restored as healthy as the other.
The Pharisees went out, and immediately conspired with the Herodians against him, how they might destroy him.

lessons.title: Peace in the storm
lessons.subtitle: Bring fear into the conversation.
lessons.artworkAlt: An empty wooden fishing boat rests on calm indigo water beneath retreating storm clouds.
lessons.summary: A storm fills the boat while Jesus sleeps. Frightened disciples wake him. Jesus stills the wind and sea, then questions their fear and lack of faith. They wonder who he is, that even wind and water obey him.

challenge.prompt: Put the crossing’s events in order.

choices.text: The wind and sea become calm

challenge.explanation: The storm leads to an urgent appeal and then calm. The disciples are left asking about Jesus’ identity and authority.

lessons.takeaway: Fear can become an honest prayer rather than silence.
lessons.application: What fear would you like to bring honestly to God today?

verses.text: On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, “Let’s go over to the other side.”
Leaving the multitude, they took him with them, even as he was, in the boat. Other small boats were also with him.
A big wind storm arose, and the waves beat into the boat, so much that the boat was already filled.
He himself was in the stern, asleep on the cushion; and they woke him up and asked him, “Teacher, don’t you care that we are dying?”
He awoke and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” The wind ceased and there was a great calm.
He said to them, “Why are you so afraid? How is it that you have no faith?”
They were greatly afraid and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”

lessons.title: Two daughters restored
lessons.subtitle: No one disappears into the crowd.
lessons.artworkAlt: A family prepares bread and a clay water cup beside a young girl’s bed in a sunlit room.
lessons.summary: Jairus asks Jesus to help his daughter. Along the way, a woman touches Jesus’ clothes and is healed. After news that the girl has died, Jesus raises her and asks that she be given food.

challenge.prompt: What does Jesus request after the girl gets up?
challenge.explanation: After restoring the girl, Jesus attends to an ordinary need: food. His care includes personal attention and practical provision.

lessons.takeaway: Care can include both deep concern and ordinary kindness.
lessons.application: Who might appreciate a meal or another practical expression of care?

verses.text: When Jesus had crossed back over in the boat to the other side, a great multitude was gathered to him; and he was by the sea.
Behold, one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, came; and seeing him, he fell at his feet
and begged him much, saying, “My little daughter is at the point of death. Please come and lay your hands on her, that she may be made healthy, and live.”
He went with him, and a great multitude followed him, and they pressed upon him on all sides.
A certain woman who had a discharge of blood for twelve years,
and had suffered many things by many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better, but rather grew worse,
having heard the things concerning Jesus, came up behind him in the crowd and touched his clothes.
For she said, “If I just touch his clothes, I will be made well.”
Immediately the flow of her blood was dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her affliction.
Immediately Jesus, perceiving in himself that the power had gone out from him, turned around in the crowd and asked, “Who touched my clothes?”
His disciples said to him, “You see the multitude pressing against you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’ ”
He looked around to see her who had done this thing.
But the woman, fearing and trembling, knowing what had been done to her, came and fell down before him, and told him all the truth.
He said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be cured of your disease.”
While he was still speaking, people came from the synagogue ruler’s house, saying, “Your daughter is dead. Why bother the Teacher any more?”
But Jesus, when he heard the message spoken, immediately said to the ruler of the synagogue, “Don’t be afraid, only believe.”
He allowed no one to follow him except Peter, James, and John the brother of James.
He came to the synagogue ruler’s house, and he saw an uproar, weeping, and great wailing.
When he had entered in, he said to them, “Why do you make an uproar and weep? The child is not dead, but is asleep.”
They ridiculed him. But he, having put them all out, took the father of the child, her mother, and those who were with him, and went in where the child was lying.
Taking the child by the hand, he said to her, “Talitha cumi!” which means, being interpreted, “Girl, I tell you, get up!”
Immediately the girl rose up and walked, for she was twelve years old. They were amazed with great amazement.
He strictly ordered them that no one should know this, and commanded that something should be given to her to eat.

lessons.title: Bread for the crowd
lessons.subtitle: Compassion makes room at the table.
lessons.artworkAlt: Five small loaves and two fish in a woven basket, with a green hillside and distant seated crowd.
lessons.summary: A large crowd gathers in a deserted place. Jesus teaches them with compassion. When food is needed, the disciples find five loaves and two fish. Jesus blesses and distributes them; everyone eats, and twelve baskets of pieces remain.

challenge.prompt: Put these moments in order.

choices.text: Find five loaves and two fish

challenge.explanation: The disciples bring what is available, distribute what Jesus gives, and gather the abundance after everyone has eaten.

lessons.takeaway: Notice a need, then consider what you can offer.
lessons.application: What resource, however ordinary, could you share with someone today?

verses.text: The apostles gathered themselves together to Jesus, and they told him all things, whatever they had done, and whatever they had taught.
He said to them, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
They went away in the boat to a deserted place by themselves.
They saw them going, and many recognized him and ran there on foot from all the cities. They arrived before them and came together to him.
Jesus came out, saw a great multitude, and he had compassion on them because they were like sheep without a shepherd; and he began to teach them many things.
When it was late in the day, his disciples came to him and said, “This place is deserted, and it is late in the day.
Send them away, that they may go into the surrounding country and villages and buy themselves bread, for they have nothing to eat.”
But he answered them, “You give them something to eat.” They asked him, “Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give them something to eat?”
He said to them, “How many loaves do you have? Go see.” When they knew, they said, “Five, and two fish.”
He commanded them that everyone should sit down in groups on the green grass.
They sat down in ranks, by hundreds and by fifties.
He took the five loaves and the two fish; and looking up to heaven, he blessed and broke the loaves, and he gave to his disciples to set before them, and he divided the two fish among them all.
They all ate and were filled.
They took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and also of the fish.
Those who ate the loaves were five thousand men.

lessons.title: A mother’s persistent appeal
lessons.subtitle: An outsider is heard.
lessons.artworkAlt: A mother sits beside her peacefully resting daughter in a modest home near the coast.
lessons.summary: A Syrophoenician mother asks Jesus to free her daughter from an unclean spirit. He speaks of children’s bread; she replies that even dogs receive crumbs. Jesus responds to her answer. At home she finds her daughter restored.

challenge.prompt: What image does the mother use in her reply?
challenge.explanation: Her reply continues Jesus’ table image. The story ends with help reaching a Gentile household across an ethnic boundary.

lessons.takeaway: An unfamiliar background need not prevent us from listening.
lessons.application: Whose perspective might you hear more patiently across a difference of background?

verses.text: From there he arose and went away into the borders of Tyre and Sidon. He entered into a house and didn’t want anyone to know it, but he couldn’t escape notice.
For a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit, having heard of him, came and fell down at his feet.
Now the woman was a Greek, a Syrophoenician by race. She begged him that he would cast the demon out of her daughter.
But Jesus said to her, “Let the children be filled first, for it is not appropriate to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”
But she answered him, “Yes, Lord. Yet even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.”
He said to her, “For this saying, go your way. The demon has gone out of your daughter.”
She went away to her house, and found the child having been laid on the bed, with the demon gone out.

lessons.title: Taken aside with care
lessons.subtitle: Personal attention matters.
lessons.artworkAlt: A quiet shaded path beside a crowded Galilean village, with a single adult resting peacefully away from the bustle.
lessons.summary: People bring a man who is deaf and has difficulty speaking to Jesus. Jesus takes him away from the crowd, attends to him, and heals him. The astonished witnesses say that Jesus has done all things well.

challenge.prompt: Where does Jesus first take the man?

choices.text: To the center of the crowd

challenge.explanation: Jesus gives the man attention away from the crowd. The encounter is personal before it becomes something others talk about.

lessons.takeaway: Consider someone’s dignity as carefully as their immediate need.
lessons.application: How could you offer help privately and respectfully rather than making someone the center of attention?

verses.text: Again he departed from the borders of Tyre and Sidon, and came to the sea of Galilee through the middle of the region of Decapolis.
They brought to him one who was deaf and had an impediment in his speech. They begged him to lay his hand on him.
He took him aside from the multitude privately and put his fingers into his ears; and he spat and touched his tongue.
Looking up to heaven, he sighed, and said to him, “Ephphatha!” that is, “Be opened!”
Immediately his ears were opened, and the impediment of his tongue was released, and he spoke clearly.
He commanded them that they should tell no one, but the more he commanded them, so much the more widely they proclaimed it.
They were astonished beyond measure, saying, “He has done all things well. He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!”

lessons.title: Seeing more clearly
lessons.subtitle: Honesty makes room for another step.
lessons.artworkAlt: A village path opens into an olive grove, with one man looking carefully toward distant figures.
lessons.summary: At Bethsaida, people bring a blind man to Jesus. Jesus leads him outside the village. After the first touch, the man reports seeing people like walking trees. Jesus touches him again, and he sees everyone clearly.

challenge.prompt: Put the man’s experience in order.

choices.text: Jesus leads him outside the village
He reports seeing people like trees

challenge.explanation: The man describes his partial sight honestly. Jesus continues attending to him until the man can see clearly.

lessons.takeaway: You can be honest about what remains unclear today.
lessons.application: What question about a passage could you admit and explore instead of pretending to understand?

verses.text: He came to Bethsaida. They brought a blind man to him and begged him to touch him.
He took hold of the blind man by the hand, and brought him out of the village. When he had spat on his eyes, and laid his hands on him, he asked him if he saw anything.
He looked up, and said, “I see men, but I see them like walking trees.”
Then again he laid his hands on his eyes. He looked intently, and was restored, and saw everyone clearly.
He sent him away to his house, saying, “Don’t enter into the village, nor tell anyone in the village.”

lessons.title: Help my unbelief
lessons.subtitle: Faith can speak honestly.
lessons.artworkAlt: A father watches over his resting son, with one hand gently placed on the boy’s head.
lessons.summary: A father brings his suffering son after the disciples cannot help him. He asks Jesus for compassion and admits both belief and unbelief. Jesus frees the boy from the spirit, raises him up, and later speaks to the disciples about prayer.

challenge.prompt: What does the father admit?

choices.text: Belief alongside a need for help with unbelief
Confidence that the disciples can heal

challenge.explanation: The father does not disguise his struggle. He brings it directly to Jesus while asking for help for his son.

lessons.takeaway: Honest prayer can include the places where trust struggles.
lessons.application: What uncertainty could you express honestly in a prayer today?

verses.text: Coming to the disciples, he saw a great multitude around them, and scribes questioning them.
Immediately all the multitude, when they saw him, were greatly amazed, and running to him, greeted him.
He asked the scribes, “What are you asking them?”
One of the multitude answered, “Teacher, I brought to you my son, who has a mute spirit;
and wherever it seizes him, it throws him down; and he foams at the mouth, grinds his teeth, and becomes rigid. I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they weren’t able.”
He answered him, “Unbelieving generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I bear with you? Bring him to me.”
They brought him to him, and when he saw him, immediately the spirit convulsed him and he fell on the ground, wallowing and foaming at the mouth.
He asked his father, “How long has it been since this has been happening to him?” He said, “From childhood.
Often it has cast him both into the fire and into the water to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.”
Jesus said to him, “If you can believe, all things are possible to him who believes.”
Immediately the father of the child cried out with tears, “I believe. Help my unbelief!”
When Jesus saw that a multitude came running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to him, “You mute and deaf spirit, I command you, come out of him, and never enter him again!”
After crying out and convulsing him greatly, it came out of him. The boy became like one dead, so much that most of them said, “He is dead.”
But Jesus took him by the hand and raised him up; and he arose.
When he had come into the house, his disciples asked him privately, “Why couldn’t we cast it out?”
He said to them, “This kind can come out by nothing but by prayer and fasting.”

lessons.title: Let the children come
lessons.subtitle: Welcome has room for the small.
lessons.artworkAlt: Children and caregivers approach an open garden courtyard together in warm, welcoming light.
lessons.summary: People bring children to Jesus, but the disciples turn them away. Jesus is indignant and tells them to allow the children to come. He speaks of receiving God’s kingdom like a child, then embraces and blesses them.

challenge.prompt: How does Jesus respond to the children?

choices.text: He asks their parents to return later
He asks the disciples to choose a few

challenge.explanation: Jesus corrects the barrier the disciples create. His welcome emphasizes receiving the kingdom, not earning a place through status.

lessons.takeaway: Welcome becomes real when we remove barriers for others.
lessons.application: Who might feel overlooked in a group you belong to, and how could you include them?

verses.text: They were bringing to him little children, that he should touch them, but the disciples rebuked those who were bringing them.
But when Jesus saw it, he was moved with indignation and said to them, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them, for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these.
Most certainly I tell you, whoever will not receive God’s Kingdom like a little child, he will in no way enter into it.”
He took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.

lessons.title: The man with many possessions
lessons.subtitle: Notice what is hard to release.
lessons.artworkAlt: A richly dressed adult stands thoughtfully beside a small chest in a stone courtyard, an open path beyond.
lessons.summary: A man asks Jesus about eternal life. Jesus looks at him with love and invites him to sell his possessions, give to the poor, and follow. The man leaves sorrowfully. Jesus then describes the difficulty of trusting in riches.

challenge.prompt: How does Jesus look at the man before challenging him?

choices.text: With approval of his financial success
With reluctance to speak with him

challenge.explanation: The difficult invitation comes with love. Jesus exposes wealth’s hold while teaching that salvation is possible with God.

lessons.takeaway: Love may invite us to examine a costly attachment.
lessons.application: What attachment might deserve a closer look as you consider generosity?

verses.text: As he was going out into the way, one ran to him, knelt before him, and asked him, “Good Teacher, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?”
Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one—God.
You know the commandments: ‘Do not murder,’ ‘Do not commit adultery,’ ‘Do not steal,’ ‘Do not give false testimony,’ ‘Do not defraud,’ ‘Honor your father and mother.’ ”
He said to him, “Teacher, I have observed all these things from my youth.”
Jesus looking at him loved him, and said to him, “One thing you lack. Go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me, taking up the cross.”
But his face fell at that saying, and he went away sorrowful, for he was one who had great possessions.
Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, “How difficult it is for those who have riches to enter into God’s Kingdom!”
The disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus answered again, “Children, how hard it is for those who trust in riches to enter into God’s Kingdom!
It is easier for a camel to go through a needle’s eye than for a rich man to enter into God’s Kingdom.”
They were exceedingly astonished, saying to him, “Then who can be saved?”
Jesus, looking at them, said, “With men it is impossible, but not with God, for all things are possible with God.”
Peter began to tell him, “Behold, we have left all and have followed you.”

Jesus said, “Most certainly I tell you, there is no one who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or land, for my sake, and for the sake of the Good News,
but he will receive one hundred times more now in this time: houses, brothers, sisters, mothers, children, and land, with persecutions; and in the age to come eternal life.
But many who are first will be last, and the last first.”

lessons.title: Greatness through service
lessons.subtitle: Leadership can take the lower place.
lessons.artworkAlt: A plain linen towel and clay pitcher beside a low dining table, sunlight highlighting humble tools of service.
lessons.summary: James and John ask for places of honor beside Jesus. The other disciples become angry. Jesus contrasts domination with service: whoever wants greatness must serve. He points to his own mission of serving and giving his life for many.

challenge.prompt: What marks greatness among Jesus’ followers?
challenge.explanation: Jesus redirects ambition toward service and grounds it in his own self-giving mission, rather than the pursuit of power.

lessons.takeaway: Use influence to meet needs rather than collect honor.
lessons.application: Where could you use responsibility or influence to make someone else’s work easier?

verses.text: James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came near to him, saying, “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we will ask.”
He said to them, “What do you want me to do for you?”
They said to him, “Grant to us that we may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left hand, in your glory.”
But Jesus said to them, “You don’t know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, and to be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?”
They said to him, “We are able.” Jesus said to them, “You shall indeed drink the cup that I drink, and you shall be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with;
but to sit at my right hand and at my left hand is not mine to give, but for whom it has been prepared.”
When the ten heard it, they began to be indignant toward James and John.
Jesus summoned them and said to them, “You know that they who are recognized as rulers over the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.
But it shall not be so among you, but whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant.
Whoever of you wants to become first among you shall be bondservant of all.
For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

lessons.title: Bartimaeus is heard
lessons.subtitle: Listen past the crowd’s dismissal.
lessons.artworkAlt: A man seated beside his discarded cloak raises one hand toward a sunlit road.
lessons.summary: Blind Bartimaeus calls to Jesus for mercy near Jericho. Many tell him to be quiet, but he keeps calling. Jesus stops, calls him forward, and asks what he wants. Bartimaeus receives sight and follows Jesus along the road.

challenge.prompt: What does Jesus do when Bartimaeus calls?

choices.text: He stops and calls him forward
He asks him to wait until later
He lets the crowd answer for him

challenge.explanation: Where the crowd tries to silence Bartimaeus, Jesus makes room for his voice and asks him to name his need.

lessons.takeaway: A voice others dismiss may deserve your careful attention.
lessons.application: Whose voice could you make room for in your next conversation?

verses.text: They came to Jericho. As he went out from Jericho with his disciples and a great multitude, the son of Timaeus, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, was sitting by the road.
When he heard that it was Jesus the Nazarene, he began to cry out and say, “Jesus, you son of David, have mercy on me!”
Many rebuked him, that he should be quiet, but he cried out much more, “You son of David, have mercy on me!”
Jesus stood still and said, “Call him.” They called the blind man, saying to him, “Cheer up! Get up. He is calling you!”
He, casting away his cloak, sprang up, and came to Jesus.
Jesus asked him, “What do you want me to do for you?” The blind man said to him, “Rabboni, that I may see again.”
Jesus said to him, “Go your way. Your faith has made you well.” Immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus on the way.

lessons.title: Two small coins
lessons.subtitle: An amount does not tell the whole story.
lessons.artworkAlt: An older woman’s hand holds two tiny brass coins beside a stone treasury opening.
lessons.summary: Jesus watches people giving at the treasury. Rich people contribute large amounts; a poor widow gives two small coins. Jesus tells his disciples that her offering is greater because she gives from poverty, putting in all she has to live on.

challenge.prompt: What difference does Jesus point out?

choices.text: What the gift costs the giver
The public praise each giver receives

challenge.explanation: Jesus sees what the amounts conceal: the widow’s vulnerable circumstances and the cost of her gift. Small does not mean insignificant.

lessons.takeaway: Look beyond visible amounts before judging another person’s contribution.
lessons.application: What quiet contribution from someone else could you notice with gratitude?

verses.text: Jesus sat down opposite the treasury and saw how the multitude cast money into the treasury. Many who were rich cast in much.
A poor widow came and she cast in two small brass coins, which equal a quadrans coin.
He called his disciples to himself and said to them, “Most certainly I tell you, this poor widow gave more than all those who are giving into the treasury,
for they all gave out of their abundance, but she, out of her poverty, gave all that she had to live on.”

lessons.title: Water at the wedding
lessons.subtitle: Ordinary obedience meets an unexpected sign.
lessons.artworkAlt: Six large stone water jars stand in a lamplit wedding courtyard beside a small pouring cup.
lessons.summary: At a wedding in Cana, the wine runs out. Jesus tells servants to fill jars with water, draw some out, and carry it to the feast’s ruler. The water has become wine—a sign that John says reveals Jesus’ glory.

challenge.prompt: Put the servants’ actions in order.

choices.text: Carry some to the feast’s ruler
